initial_relationship: Newly married by arrangement
how_they_meet: They do not meet in the film; the arranged marriage has already taken place when it opens, and the whole relationship is conducted after the wedding.
who_initiates: Neither; the families arranged the match
courtship_pattern: Courtship runs backwards, after marriage rather than before it. Prem approaches his own wife with the awkwardness of a stranger, and the tenderness between them grows only as he stops treating her as an obligation.
emotional_dynamic: Immature affection on his side and mounting frustration on hers, with neither able to say plainly what they want from the other.
pair_conflict: Prem will not take his wife's side against his mother, and Indu will not go on living in a household where she is displaced.
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is real but not hostile: it comes from Prem's failure to act as a husband rather than from any dislike between them. It accumulates through small domestic humiliations and culminates in Indu leaving for her family, which is a rupture rather than a quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Prem's mother arrives and takes over the running of the household, displacing Indu in her own home. She is not malicious in the manner of a villain, but her presence is sustained and is the direct cause of the separation.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is the film's whole subject, but Prem is not courting: he is a husband learning the job. There is no pursuit, no rebellion for love and no romantic heroism, and his emotional openness arrives only at the end. The role belongs to the domestic register rather than the lover-boy one.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Naidu play the awkwardness of two people married before they were acquainted, and the register is deliberately underplayed rather than charged; what works is the growing ease between them, not any initial spark.
actor_transformation: Prem grows from a man who defers to his mother into one who can choose his wife; the film is named for the role he finally accepts.
female_transformation: Indu moves from silent endurance to leaving, and returns only once the household she is returning to has changed.
relationship_outcome: Reconciled, with Prem having acquired the maturity the marriage required of him.
relationship_analysis: The film is unusual in Kapoor's early work for treating marriage as the subject rather than the reward. The obstacle is neither a villain nor a class barrier but the husband's own immaturity, and the resolution is a change in him rather than a removal of some external impediment. Indu's departure is the film's strongest action and it is hers, which lifts the female agency score above what the period would predict.
critical_reading: Read now, the film's sympathies sit more with Indu than its own framing admits: it presents Prem's education as the story while the concrete grievance, a wife displaced in her home by her mother-in-law, is entirely hers. The swami's counsel resolves the marriage by improving the husband's attitude rather than by addressing the arrangement that produced the problem.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Anwar sees Sahida and falls in love with her; the article's storyline gives no more circumstance than that.
courtship_pattern: Compressed and direct: he sees her, loves her and proposes marriage, with no obstacle raised between the two of them.
emotional_dynamic: Young, cheerful and uncomplicated, set deliberately against the older generation's ruinous entanglement.
pair_conflict: None between the couple; the threat comes entirely from Nawab's suspicion of his brother.
pair_friction_explanation: The article's storyline records no disagreement of any kind between Anwar and Sahida. Their function in the film is to be the uncomplicated pairing against which the Nawab, his wife and Benazir are measured.
external_opposition_explanation: Nawab is told that Anwar has been visiting his mistress Benazir and then sees Benazir in his brother's arms. The resulting rupture between the brothers threatens the marriage Anwar has proposed, though the storyline does not follow it through.
lover_boy_explanation: Within a brief part Anwar is defined almost entirely by falling in love and proposing, which is the lover-boy function in miniature. The score is held down because the role is short and carries no sustained courtship, sacrifice or romantic heroism.
chemistry_explanation: A retrospective notice quoted in the film article holds that Kapoor and Tanuja make only brief appearances but do justice to their roles as a beautiful young cheerful pair, which is an assessment of the pairing rather than of either performance alone.
actor_transformation: None recorded; the part is too brief for an arc.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: Not stated by the article's storyline summary, which stops at Nawab's discovery.
relationship_analysis: This is the secondary romance of a film whose centre is the Nawab's relationship with the courtesan Benazir. Its structural job is contrast: a young, sanctioned, uncomplicated attachment beside an older, adulterous and socially impossible one. Kapoor is not the film's romantic lead and the pairing is not developed, which is why almost every categorical field here is recorded as unclear rather than guessed.
critical_reading: The pairing is too lightly sketched to carry much modern reading, but the structure is worth noting: Sahida exists to be proposed to, and the dramatic interest of the misunderstanding belongs wholly to the two brothers, with the courtesan Benazir positioned as the thing they contest rather than a party to it.

initial_relationship: Strangers from different worlds
how_they_meet: Sanju attaches himself to the Buckinghams' travelling Shakespeare company as it tours India, and courts the troupe's daughter.
courtship_pattern: A rich man's pursuit conducted at his own convenience, around a touring schedule and around the other woman he does not give up.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine affection on both sides, undercut throughout by his refusal to choose and by her growing understanding of what that means.
pair_conflict: Sanju will not relinquish Manjula, and Lizzie will not go on sharing him.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no hostility between them and little open quarrelling; the friction is the steady pressure of Manjula's continuing presence, which Lizzie registers and Sanju declines to resolve. It is corrosive rather than combative.
external_opposition_explanation: Manjula's established claim on Sanju is the direct obstacle, and she acts on it. Behind that sits the larger displacement the film is about: English theatre in India is dying, the Buckinghams must keep moving, and the Hindi film industry that Manjula embodies is what is replacing them.
lover_boy_explanation: Sanju is a romantic figure and courtship occupies most of his screen time, but he is a playboy rather than a devotee: there is no sacrifice, no rebellion and no constancy. He is charming and emotionally available without being committed, which is the lover-boy surface without its substance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Felicity Kendal play an easy, unforced attraction that makes his failure to choose read as carelessness rather than coldness, which is what the film needs; the warmth is real enough that her departure registers as a loss.
actor_transformation: None. Sanju ends the film as he began it, which is the point being made about him.
female_transformation: Lizzie moves from infatuation to a clear sight of her position, and acts on it by leaving India.
relationship_outcome: Ends with Lizzie's departure; the relationship is abandoned rather than resolved.
relationship_analysis: The romance is the personal register of the film's historical argument. Sanju can hold both women because he belongs to the ascendant world and neither needs him; Lizzie belongs to a troupe whose audiences are vanishing, and her leaving is as much economic as romantic. The pairing carries an unusually high female agency score for Kapoor's 1960s work because the decisive action of the film is hers.
critical_reading: Modern readings tend to be harder on Sanju than the film is: he is indulged as a charming idler while the costs of his indecision fall entirely on the two women, and the film's sympathy for Lizzie does not extend to naming his behaviour. Manjula, meanwhile, is written close to the jealous-film-star stereotype even as the film credits her industry with displacing the Buckinghams.

initial_relationship: Existing affair, already running when the film begins
how_they_meet: Not shown; the relationship predates the story.
courtship_pattern: No courtship. The relationship is an established arrangement between a wealthy idler and a film star, which Sanju continues while pursuing Lizzie.
emotional_dynamic: Possessive on her side, casual on his; she treats his attention as hers by right and moves to protect it.
pair_conflict: Lizzie. Manjula's whole conflict with Sanju is over the other woman.
pair_friction_explanation: Recurring and pointed conflict, all of it about Sanju's divided attention. It stops short of rupture because neither party treats the relationship as a commitment that could be broken.
external_opposition_explanation: Little external force acts on this pair. The obstacle to it is Lizzie, which makes the opposition internal to the triangle rather than imposed from outside it.
lover_boy_explanation: Sanju's conduct here is the opposite of the archetype: an arrangement maintained out of convenience, with no courtship, devotion or openness. It is included in the scoring because it is a real and consequential relationship, not because it is romantic.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Jaffrey plays Manjula with a hauteur that makes Sanju look slight beside her, and the friction between them is more interesting to watch than the affection; the pairing reads as habit rather than attraction, which appears to be the intention.
actor_transformation: None.
female_transformation: None; Manjula ends in possession of the field.
relationship_outcome: Continues. Manjula keeps Sanju, largely by outlasting Lizzie.
relationship_analysis: A second pairing row is warranted here because the relationship is consequential rather than decorative: Manjula is the reason Lizzie leaves, and she acts to make it so. The pairing also sets a pattern worth tracking across the filmography, in which Kapoor's character maintains a prior attachment while courting the film's heroine.
critical_reading: Manjula is written as the glamorous obstacle and given the period's stock attributes of the jealous star, but the film also lets her be right: Sanju is hers and is behaving badly. The interest of the part now is that its antagonism is entirely justified by the plot even as the film frames it as an impediment to the romance the audience is meant to want.

actress_prominence: Female lead of one of three strands
initial_relationship: College acquaintances, already in love when the film's present begins
how_they_meet: They met at college; Renu has loved him since then.
who_initiates: Renu, whose attachment predates and outlasts his ability to act on it
courtship_pattern: Settled affection rather than pursuit. The obstacle is never her feeling, which is constant, but his circumstances.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and mutual, strained by his embarrassment at what he has been reduced to.
pair_conflict: Almost none between them; Vijay's poverty and his refusal to be pitied are the nearest thing to a quarrel.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple are aligned throughout. What little tension exists comes from Vijay's shame at driving a car for a living while holding a degree, not from any disagreement with Renu, who never wavers.
external_opposition_explanation: Renu's foster brother Ravi objects to the attachment and quarrels with her over it. Behind that sits the real barrier: Vijay is a graduate working as a chauffeur, supporting a mother dying of cancer, and is in no position to marry into the Khanna household.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay is the romantic one of the three brothers and the strand is built on devotion under economic humiliation, but the film's weight sits on the family's separation and reunion. His defining act is filial rather than romantic: he drives to pay for his mother's treatment.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Tagore play the ease of an established college attachment rather than the charge of a new one, and the warmth holds up against the film's much noisier strands; their scenes read as the least performed thing in a highly performed film.
actor_transformation: Little. Vijay is constant; what changes is his situation once the family is restored.
female_transformation: Renu holds to the attachment against her foster brother's objection, which is the extent of her arc.
relationship_outcome: Cleared to marry once the brothers are reunited and Vijay's circumstances change.
relationship_analysis: In the film that established the Hindi multi-starrer, Kapoor's is the romantic strand and it is deliberately the quietest of the three. The pairing has almost no internal friction, which throws the entire dramatic load onto class and family, and makes it an early clear instance of the pattern that dominates his 1970s work: high external opposition, near-zero pair friction, and romance subordinated to a family plot.
critical_reading: The class obstacle is presented as a misunderstanding to be dissolved by the plot's coincidences rather than as a structural fact, and it is resolved by restoring Vijay to a wealthy family rather than by anyone accepting a chauffeur. Renu's constancy is admirable but entirely reactive; she waits, and the narrative rewards her for waiting.

initial_relationship: Houseboat owner and holidaying tenant
how_they_meet: Rita, a Bombay heiress on holiday in Kashmir, rents the houseboat Raja owns and lives on with his small sister.
who_initiates: Raja, after a period of misunderstandings gives way to friendship
courtship_pattern: Slow and deferential, conducted across a season on the water; she returns the following year as promised, and he declares himself only when she does.
emotional_dynamic: Unguarded devotion on his side and delighted recognition on hers, with the imbalance of wealth present but never weaponised between them.
pair_conflict: The makeover. Rita asks Raja to change his dress and manners for her father's world, and he cannot bear watching her dance with other men in it.
pair_friction_explanation: For most of the film the couple are entirely aligned, but the quarrel at the Bombay party is a genuine interpersonal rupture rather than an external obstacle: she asks him to become someone else, he agrees, and he leaves when he finds he cannot. The friction is real, brief and decisive.
external_opposition_explanation: Raj Bahadur engineers the separation deliberately. He tells his daughter that a Kashmiri boatman cannot adapt to their ways, stages the party at which the quarrel occurs, and is later overheard admitting he knew Raja would not tolerate it. The class barrier is not incidental; it is actively worked by her father.
lover_boy_explanation: This is the role that made Kapoor a romantic star. Raja's identity is entirely organised around loving Rita: he has no other plot, no rival ambition and no function in the film outside the courtship. He is emotionally open throughout, sacrifices his own terms and then refuses to, and the songs are built on him. It falls short of ten only because his final act is to leave rather than to pursue.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The pairing is the reason the film worked and the reason Kapoor became a star on it: his unpolished warmth against Nanda's poised amusement gives the class gap an affectionate rather than a pitying register, and the Kashmir songs are filmed as a two-hander.
actor_transformation: Raja submits to being remade for her world, discovers what it costs him, and takes himself back; the film endorses the refusal.
female_transformation: Rita moves from asking him to change to understanding that she was manoeuvred into asking, and then chooses his life over her father's.
relationship_outcome: She comes to the railway station and he pulls her onto the moving train.
relationship_analysis: The defining romance of Kapoor's early career and the template for the persona the rest of the filmography either extends or reacts against: a poor, guileless, entirely devoted man loved by a rich woman, with the obstacle placed squarely in her family and her class rather than between the couple. It is also, unusually for the period, a film that resolves the class problem by having the wealthy partner cross over rather than by elevating the poor one.
critical_reading: The makeover sequence reads differently now than it plays: the film treats Raja's refusal to be assimilated as integrity, but the quarrel is triggered by his objection to Rita dancing with other men, which the narrative endorses as wounded love rather than examining as possessiveness. Rita's final choice is genuine agency, though it is framed as a woman giving up her world for a man rather than as two people meeting.
romantic_songs: Ye Samaa Samaa Hai Pyar Ka; Na Na Karte Pyar Tumhin Se; Pardesiyon Se Na Ankhiyan Milana; Ek Tha Gul Aur Ek Thi Bulbul; Affoo Khudaya

actress_prominence: One of two sisters sharing the female lead
initial_relationship: Employer's daughter and the assistant manager dismissed for misbehaving with her
how_they_meet: Ashok manages her father's property; he is fired for misbehaving with both daughters and pitches a tent in the front garden in protest.
courtship_pattern: Farcical siege. Having been thrown out, he camps on the lawn, and the courtship proceeds through comic provocation and an elaborate imposture staged for her father's benefit.
emotional_dynamic: Teasing and broad, pitched for comedy rather than feeling.
pair_conflict: Little between them once the teasing resolves; the difficulty is entirely in getting her father's consent.
pair_friction_explanation: The early antagonism is played as farce and dissolves quickly. What remains is mild and comic rather than a genuine incompatibility, and the couple are aligned for most of the film's running time.
external_opposition_explanation: Ramlal intends both daughters to marry into wealthier families and dismisses Ashok, the son of a poor schoolteacher, as a prospect. The fraudulent billionaire father is invented to clear precisely this obstacle, and its exposure lands Ashok in police custody.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is Ashok's whole plot and he goes to elaborate lengths for it, but the register is comic rather than devotional, and he shares the film with two other couples and with Mehmood's comedy. He is a romantic lead in an ensemble farce rather than a romantic hero.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film's energy sits with Kishore Kumar and Mehmood rather than with the romance, and Kapoor and Rajasree function as the straight couple around which the farce is built; the pairing is pleasant and lightly drawn rather than charged.
actor_transformation: None; the imposture is exposed and forgiven without changing him.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: Married, in the general reconciliation that pairs off all three couples.
relationship_analysis: A subordinate romance inside an ensemble comedy, and useful chiefly as a contrast with the same year's Jab Jab Phool Khile: the identical class obstacle, a poor suitor and a rich father, is resolved here by fraud and farce rather than by the woman crossing over. The deception is directed at the father rather than at Nirmala, which keeps the pairing's health score from falling further.
critical_reading: The premise that Ashok is dismissed for misbehaving with both daughters and then rewarded with marriage to one of them is the film's least defensible move, presented entirely as comedy. Nirmala has almost no part in her own courtship: the decisive manoeuvres are conducted between men, and her consent is assumed rather than sought.

initial_relationship: One of three suitors, initially rejected by her parents
how_they_meet: Anwar is presented as a suitor for Nishat, the daughter of a Delhi Khan Bahadur, and is approved once the family takes him for a Nawab's son.
courtship_pattern: A formal suit conducted through the parents and then, after a few meetings, a genuine attachment between the couple themselves.
emotional_dynamic: Straightforward affection on both sides, shadowed by a secret he carries and she does not know.
pair_conflict: Nothing between them; the whole danger is the concealed fact of his father's origins.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple are aligned throughout the synopsis. Such conflict as exists is between Anwar and his rivals, or between his family's pretensions and the truth, rather than between him and Nishat.
external_opposition_explanation: Two rival suitors with genuine noble pedigrees compete for Nishat, her parents assess suitors by birth, and the discovery that Anwar's father was a barber who bought the title of Nawab with lottery winnings reaches the family on the wedding day itself.
lover_boy_explanation: Anwar's function in the film is to win Nishat and he has no other plot; the courtship is his entire arc and the attachment is sincere. The score stops short of the Jab Jab Phool Khile register because the obstacle is an inherited imposture he is passively carrying rather than a devotion he actively proves.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Nanda were by this point a proven pairing and the film leans on that familiarity rather than building the attraction; the ease between them is the film's most reliable asset, in a synopsis that otherwise turns on plot mechanics.
actor_transformation: Not recorded; the synopsis stops before any resolution.
female_transformation: Not recorded.
relationship_outcome: Not stated. The article's synopsis is written as a teaser and breaks off at the wedding-day revelation, asking whether the marriage will proceed.
relationship_analysis: The second of three Kapoor and Nanda pairings in this batch and a near-inversion of Jab Jab Phool Khile: there the poor man is honest about what he is and the rich family manoeuvres against him, here the man passes as noble and the deception is his family's. The class barrier is identical; what changes is who is concealing what.
critical_reading: The film's anxiety is entirely about birth being discovered rather than about the dishonesty itself, and Nishat, who is the person actually deceived, is positioned as the prize whose reaction the film withholds rather than as the injured party. The synopsis's closing question is addressed to the audience's interest in the match, not to her.

initial_relationship: Neighbours; she believes he is stalking her
how_they_meet: Sapna is the wealthy neighbour of the man calling himself Gopal Mittal, and finds him annoying and intrusive before she is charmed by him.
who_initiates: Gopal, by a persistent attention she initially reads as harassment
courtship_pattern: Pursuit against resistance, converted into marriage quickly, with the real relationship conducted afterwards under the shadow of what she learns.
emotional_dynamic: Charm on his side and a mounting, rational terror on hers once she knows what he was tried for.
pair_conflict: Sapna cannot establish whether the man she has married murdered his first wife and intends to murder her.
pair_friction_explanation: Substantial and sustained mistrust, and unlike most of Kapoor's pairings in this period it sits squarely between the couple rather than outside them. Her suspicion is the film's engine, and his changeable behaviour feeds it deliberately.
external_opposition_explanation: Sapna's brother Pran wants her married to Prem, and both men threaten to kill her when she chooses otherwise. An actual attempt is made on her life during the honeymoon, and the conspiracy against her is external to the marriage even though the film arranges every clue to point at her husband.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor is the romantic lead and the courtship drives the first act, but the role's function is suspicion rather than devotion: the performance is built to keep the audience uncertain about him. Romantic heroism is displaced by ambiguity, which is the opposite of the lover-boy contract.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The pairing is deliberately uncomfortable: Kapoor plays charm as something that might be a mask, and Tagore plays attraction curdling into fear, so what the film wants is unease rather than warmth, and the two register it well enough that the suspicion holds.
actor_transformation: Moves from a man hiding an acquittal under an alias to one publicly cleared, which permits the marriage to stand.
female_transformation: Sapna goes from a woman who dismisses him to one who marries him to one who must decide whether to believe him, and survives the attempt on her life.
relationship_outcome: The conspiracy is exposed, Gopal is cleared and the marriage holds.
relationship_analysis: The most internally conflicted pairing in this batch and a marked departure from the Kapoor template: here the friction score exceeds most of his 1960s romances because the doubt is between husband and wife rather than imposed by a father. It is also the first of several films in which he plays charm as potentially sinister, a register the industry rarely asked of him again.
critical_reading: The film's treatment of Sapna's initial reading of him as a stalker is instructive: her discomfort is played as a misunderstanding she must be talked out of, and the narrative rewards persistence that it has already shown her experiencing as intrusion. That her later fear turns out to be misdirected does not entirely settle the earlier pattern.

initial_relationship: Tourist and hired guide
how_they_meet: Polly, stranded in Singapore by the sudden death of the aunt she was companion to, takes up with Amaz, a local tour guide.
courtship_pattern: Deliberately kept at arm's length. The film describes the romance in those terms itself: an attachment explored rather than consummated, inside a few weeks of unexpected freedom.
emotional_dynamic: Gentle and exploratory, with the emotional weight falling on her emergence rather than on the couple.
pair_conflict: Almost none; the limit on the relationship is circumstance and Polly's inexperience rather than any conflict between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No antagonism is recorded between the pair. The relationship is constrained rather than contested, and the constraint is situational.
external_opposition_explanation: The obstacles are the proprieties surrounding a young Englishwoman abroad, the temporary nature of her stay and the social distance between a tourist and a local guide, none of them dramatised as active opposition by a named party.
lover_boy_explanation: Amaz is charming, attentive and the film's romantic interest, but the part is a supporting function in someone else's coming-of-age: he neither pursues nor sacrifices, and the film ends with him left behind rather than chosen.
chemistry_explanation: A contemporary notice quoted in the film article found Kapoor to have plenty of charm but to be altogether too wholesome for Amaz, and judged Mills unable to supply Polly's necessary touch of malice, concluding that the whole had the air of glossy magazine romance. The score follows that assessment rather than an interpretive reading.
actor_transformation: None recorded.
female_transformation: Polly moves from a repressed paid companion to a young woman with some sense of her own appetites; the film is named for that change.
relationship_outcome: Ends with her departure; the romance is a passage in her life rather than a destination.
relationship_analysis: One of the few pairings in the filmography where Kapoor is the romantic object rather than the romantic agent, and where the woman's development is the subject. The arm's-length quality is structural, not a failure of the writing: the film requires Amaz to be an opportunity Polly takes rather than a man who takes her.
critical_reading: The casting of an Indian actor as the sexually suggestive local attachment for a young Englishwoman abroad carries the period's exoticising conventions, and the review quoted in the article effectively concedes the point by complaining that Kapoor is too wholesome for a part written to be faintly dangerous. The film wants the frisson of transgression without committing to it.

initial_relationship: Strangers, introduced by a case of mistaken identity
how_they_meet: Archana means to complain to the principal about Rakesh, who has been tormenting her, and complains about Kamal by mistake, the two being identical.
who_initiates: Archana, through the error that brings them together, and then Kamal
courtship_pattern: An apology that turns into an attachment, conducted under continual sabotage from his double.
emotional_dynamic: Straightforward warmth between the couple, set against a persistent external threat wearing her husband's face.
pair_conflict: Not between them by choice: the crisis is Archana's inability to know whether the man in her house is her husband.
pair_friction_explanation: Kamal and Archana are aligned whenever they are actually dealing with each other. The mistrust that dominates the last act is manufactured by the double and by a superior officer's report of Kamal's death, not by anything either of them does.
external_opposition_source: Existing relationship; Villain; War or politics
external_opposition_explanation: Rakesh plots to kidnap Kamal and marry Archana in his place, is seized by his own men by mistake, follows Kamal into the army, and fights him on a riverbank. The war separates the couple, a death notice is delivered, and Kamal is arrested and faces ten years for impersonation and rape before Rakesh appears to testify.
lover_boy_explanation: Kamal is decent, devoted and defined by the marriage, but the film's second half converts him from a lover into a man trying to prove his own identity. The romantic content is displaced by the impersonation thriller, and the double role splits the audience's attention between courtship and menace.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor carries most of the film's charge against himself rather than opposite Babita, and the pairing is warm but conventional; its best stretch is the testing sequence, where her wariness gives the relationship more to play than the courtship did.
actor_transformation: Kamal moves from an orphan with no standing to a husband, and then to a man who must prove he is himself.
female_transformation: Archana moves from a student lodging a complaint to a wife who devises tests to establish who is living in her house, which is the most active thing anyone does in the last act.
relationship_outcome: Vindicated when the real Rakesh appears and testifies; the couple reconcile and forgive him.
relationship_analysis: The interest of the pairing is that the antagonist is played by the same actor, so the threat to the marriage is literally the husband's face used against it. Archana's testing of the man in her house is a rare instance in this period of Kapoor's filmography where the woman holds the investigative function, and it lifts an otherwise conventional romance.
critical_reading: The plot turns on Rakesh's plan to obtain a wife by impersonation, and on a charge of rape by deception that the film raises and then disposes of as a misunderstanding once the double reappears. The resolution has the couple forgive him, which reads now as a considerable indulgence of a man whose scheme was to take Archana's consent under false pretences.

initial_relationship: Strangers; a stranded traveller and the village girl who shelters him
how_they_meet: Kumar's car breaks down near her village and Rekha invites him to stay at her house, having nowhere else to offer him.
who_initiates: Kumar, who contrives to stop at her village again on his way back
courtship_pattern: A hospitable acquaintance that becomes mutual attraction, then a formal approach to her mother, and finally a courtship resumed on a false premise.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine attachment on both sides, poisoned by his decision to let her believe something untrue rather than lose her.
pair_conflict: Kumar allows Rekha to believe he is the Amar she was married to as a child, then tells her the truth and asks her to accept him anyway.
pair_friction_explanation: The central breach is his, and it is deliberate: he produces a driving licence showing his full name is Amar Kumar to let a false conclusion stand. When he admits it, she is enraged and leaves intending to kill herself. This is interpersonal damage, not external obstruction.
external_opposition_explanation: Rekha was married in childhood to a man she has never seen, a custom she regards as binding absolutely; the real Amar is already happily married to Lata, whose household Rekha then enters; and tensions build there over her presence. The obstacle is a social institution rather than a person opposing the match.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is the film and Kumar is a poet whose attachment is sincere, but the role's defining act is a deception committed to secure the woman, followed by collapse into drink. That is romantic obsession shading into self-interest rather than the devotional register of the archetype.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Asha Parekh play the early village scenes with a lightness that makes the later betrayal land, and her enactment of a woman bound by a marriage she cannot remember gives the pairing a weight the courtship alone would not carry.
actor_transformation: From a man who arranges his friend's marriage honourably and promises to stand as the bride's family, to one who deceives the woman he loves, to one drinking in self-reproach.
female_transformation: Rekha moves from accepting her fate, to believing she has found her childhood husband, to discovering the deception and leaving with the intention of ending her life.
relationship_outcome: Not stated. The cached plot summary breaks off mid-sentence as Rekha leaves the house.
relationship_analysis: The most ethically compromised of Kapoor's 1960s romances, and the one where the pair friction score is driven almost entirely by his own conduct rather than by an opposing family. The film's title refers to the giving away of a daughter, and its subject is what child marriage does to a woman who takes the obligation seriously; the romance is the instrument for examining that rather than the point.
critical_reading: The film frames Kumar's deception as the desperation of a man in love and reserves its moral attention for Rekha's fidelity to a marriage contracted for her in infancy. A modern reading reverses the emphasis: the woman's consent is manipulated twice, once by the custom and once by the man who exploits a coincidence of names, and the narrative punishes her with attempted suicide while his penalty is drink.

initial_relationship: Strangers who meet repeatedly under different names he gives her
how_they_meet: Seema meets him in Ooty as Pyarelal, meets him again a year later when he introduces himself as Jhatpat Singh, the man she was betrothed to in childhood, and encounters him a third time as her grandfather's estate manager.
courtship_pattern: A courtship conducted across three identities, in which each new meeting requires her to revise who he is.
emotional_dynamic: Teasing and musical, with real feeling surviving the succession of impostures.
pair_conflict: She changes her mind about him when the real Jhatpat Singh appears and exposes the second identity as false.
pair_friction_explanation: Recurring misunderstandings, all of them generated by his aliases, and a period in which she withdraws after the imposture is exposed. The conflict is real but comic in register and is never a fundamental incompatibility.
external_opposition_explanation: Shankar plants his own son as Ranjit Singh's lost grandson to take the estate, and Ranjit Singh, persuaded, intends Seema to marry that impostor. The family's estrangement from Jamuna and the fire that killed Sunder's father set the whole obstruction in motion.
lover_boy_explanation: A Nasir Hussain musical romance built to the pattern of Tumsa Nahin Dekha, in which the hero's charm, the songs and the courtship carry the film. Sunder is emotionally open and persistent and the romance is his principal plot, though it shares the film with a substantial inheritance intrigue and the recovery of his mother's sanity.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film is constructed around R. D. Burman's songs and the pairing is at its best inside them; Kapoor's lightness suits the alias comedy, and Asha Parekh gives Seema enough scepticism that the repeated deceptions do not make her look foolish.
actor_transformation: From a man with no known parentage passing under borrowed names to an acknowledged heir marrying under his own.
female_transformation: Seema moves between suitors as the identities resolve, and is finally married to the man she first met.
relationship_outcome: Married, as the family reunites and Jamuna's sanity returns.
relationship_analysis: The deception here is structurally different from Kanyadaan's, though both involve Kapoor letting a woman believe he is someone else: this one is played entirely for comedy and costs her nothing, because the identity he eventually claims is his own by right. It is the lighter treatment of a device the filmography returns to repeatedly in this decade.
critical_reading: Seema is moved between three men by other people's schemes and her own information problem, and the film treats her successive reassignments as comic reversals rather than as anything she has a stake in. The resolution restores the patriarchal estate and delivers her to the legitimate heir, which is the outcome the plot was always arranging.

initial_relationship: He loves her; she has already chosen another man
how_they_meet: Not detailed by the article's brief plot section, which opens with Pritam already in love with Deepali.
courtship_pattern: Indirect. Rather than court Deepali against her existing choice, Pritam wins over her uncle through a series of comic encounters and uses that backing to win her.
emotional_dynamic: Light comic pursuit; the film is brief and pitched throughout for amusement.
pair_conflict: Her prior commitment to Ajit is the only thing standing between them.
pair_friction_explanation: The obstacle is her preference for another man rather than hostility toward Pritam, and it is dissolved by comedy rather than confrontation. Nothing in the article's summary suggests antagonism between the two.
external_opposition_explanation: Ajit is the established suitor Deepali has chosen as her life partner, and her uncle's approval is the gate through which any rival must pass. Both are obstacles outside the couple, and Pritam addresses the second in order to defeat the first.
lover_boy_explanation: Pritam has no function in the film other than to win Deepali; the entire running time is courtship and the persistence is the character. The score is held below the top band because the pursuit is comic rather than devotional and involves no sacrifice or rebellion.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The second Kapoor and Babita pairing in two years, played in a lighter key than Haseena Maan Jayegi and with less for either to do; the film's comedy runs through Om Prakash and Rajendra Nath rather than through the couple.
actor_transformation: None; persistence is rewarded without requiring him to change.
female_transformation: Deepali transfers her choice from Ajit to Pritam, which the summary presents as an outcome rather than a decision.
relationship_outcome: Pritam wins Deepali's love with her uncle's help.
relationship_analysis: A slight film, and its interest for this project is structural: the courtship is routed through a male relative rather than conducted with the woman, so the romance is settled between men and delivered to her. Female agency is scored low for exactly that reason, and the pattern recurs across the lighter comedies of this period.
critical_reading: Deepali has made a choice before the film begins and the plot's business is overturning it without ever treating that choice as having weight. The uncle's endorsement functions as the real consent, which is a fair summary of how the period's romantic comedies distribute authority over a woman's marriage.

initial_relationship: A princess and a servant impersonating his princely employer
how_they_meet: Raju is made by his employer, Prince Pratap Singh, to impersonate him in front of Princess Poonam.
who_initiates: Raju, though inside a deception imposed on him
courtship_pattern: A courtship conducted entirely in a borrowed identity, with the man unable to be loved as himself for as long as it lasts.
emotional_dynamic: Sincere attachment on his side under an assumed name, and hesitant then genuine feeling on hers for a man who does not exist.
pair_conflict: The impersonation, which makes every exchange between them false in a way only he knows.
pair_friction_explanation: No hostility between the pair, but a structural deceit that sits between them throughout and which the article's summary treats as the film's central question. The friction is the lie rather than any incompatibility.
external_opposition_explanation: Raju was raised in an orphanage and has no birth, standing or money; Poonam is a princess. The employer who ordered the impersonation and the royal household around her constitute the barrier, and the summary poses the class question directly as the film's unresolved problem.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is the whole film and Raju's dream of living like a king is fulfilled in the form of being loved by a princess. The role is squarely romantic, but the devotion is compromised by the imposture at its centre, which keeps it below the Jab Jab Phool Khile register of transparent constancy.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The third Kapoor and Nanda pairing in five years and the one that leans hardest on their established rapport, since the plot gives Poonam little to do but respond; the familiarity does most of the work the writing does not.
actor_transformation: From an orphan playing at royalty to a man who must be accepted, if he is accepted, without the disguise.
female_transformation: Poonam moves from hesitation to love, and is left facing the question of whether that love survives the truth.
relationship_outcome: Not stated. The article's plot section ends on the rhetorical question of whether Poonam will still love Raju once she knows he is a pauper.
relationship_analysis: The third Kapoor and Nanda film in this batch and the clearest statement of the class romance in its deceptive variant: where Jab Jab Phool Khile put a poor man honestly before a rich family and let the woman cross to him, this one hides the poverty inside a borrowed title and makes the revelation the climax. Taken together the three films map most of the positions available to the period's class romance.
critical_reading: The film's question, whether a princess will love a pauper, is posed as a test of her character rather than as a problem with the arrangement that made him impersonate someone else in the first place. Poonam is courted under false pretences on her own estate and the narrative's interest is in her reaction to the disclosure rather than in the wrong done to her.

initial_relationship: Long-standing friends, now engaged with her mother's consent
how_they_meet: They are old friends when the film opens; no meeting is dramatised.
who_initiates: Neither; the attachment predates the story and the engagement is already settled
courtship_pattern: No courtship. The film is about an engagement being undermined rather than a romance being formed.
emotional_dynamic: Deep mutual trust, deliberately eroded from outside until Neeta repeats the accusation to his face.
pair_conflict: Neeta's single confrontation over the property documents, and Sudhir's refusal to stay once she has made it.
pair_friction_explanation: For most of the film the couple are entirely aligned and Neeta actively resists the poison being fed to her. The friction is concentrated in one scene and its aftermath: she accuses him, he is proved innocent immediately, and his wounded withdrawal is what keeps them apart rather than any continuing quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Naina, Neeta's cousin, wants Sudhir for herself and conducts a sustained campaign to convince Neeta that he is a fortune hunter, culminating in staging the visit to the lawyer. It is the entire obstacle, and it ends only with her suicide and confession.
lover_boy_explanation: Sudhir's defining act is refusing to touch Neeta's money and quietly signing it to her cousin, which is devotion demonstrated rather than declared. The courtship is already complete when the film starts, which holds the score below the pursuing-hero register, but the role is organised entirely around the relationship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The fourth Kapoor and Nanda pairing and the most domestic; there is little for either to play beyond steady affection, and the film's energy belongs to Kumari Naaz's Naina, whose scheming drives every scene of consequence.
actor_transformation: None; Sudhir is the fixed point the film tests.
female_transformation: Neeta moves from unshakeable trust through one failure of it to remorse and an apology.
relationship_outcome: Reconciled after Naina's dying confession and Anil's account of the manipulation.
relationship_analysis: A pure instance of the manipulated-couple structure: the pair have no incompatibility at all, and the whole drama is imported by a third party with a motive. It also shows the period's standard treatment of a poor man engaged to a propertied woman, where the plot must prove his disinterest in her money explicitly and on paper before the marriage can proceed.
critical_reading: The film resolves its problem by killing the rival woman, who is given a motive, a confession and a suicide inside a few minutes so that the couple can be restored without anyone else bearing responsibility. Neeta's one moment of doubt is treated as a wrong requiring apology, rather than as a reasonable response to evidence she had been shown deliberately.

initial_relationship: Strangers who meet by chance
how_they_meet: A chance meeting between an assistant scientist and an established stage dancer and singer.
courtship_pattern: Brief and uncontested: they meet, fall in love, his mother approves and they marry. The film's interest begins afterwards.
emotional_dynamic: Harmonious for several months, then a slow accumulation of grievance on both sides as his laboratory and her stage compete for the marriage.
pair_conflict: Anjana gives up performing for the marriage, takes it up again when Shekhar's work absorbs him, and he resents her doing so.
pair_friction_explanation: Sustained and entirely internal: recurring arguments over her return to the stage that escalate to a decision to live separately. There is no villain, no family objection after the mother's approval and no external obstacle at all, which makes this one of the few pairings in the filmography where the friction score exceeds the opposition score.
external_opposition_explanation: Almost none. Shekhar's mother approves the match at the outset and later provides the occasion for the reconciliation; the pressure on the marriage is generated inside it.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is over within minutes and what follows is a study of a husband who takes his wife's sacrifice as settled. There is no pursuit, no devotion under obstacle and no romantic heroism; the register is domestic, as in The Householder.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Hema Malini are better in the argument scenes than in the courtship, which the film hurries through; the pairing works as a marriage being negotiated rather than as an attraction.
actor_transformation: Shekhar comes to see that his absence, not her career, was the problem.
female_transformation: Anjana gives up her work, takes it back, and ends with both the marriage and the stage.
relationship_outcome: They resume living together for his mother's sake and rediscover what the marriage was missing.
relationship_analysis: The clearest early example of a pattern worth tracking: when Kapoor plays a husband rather than a suitor, pair friction rises sharply and external opposition collapses to almost nothing. Abhinetri and The Householder are structurally the same film, and both score female agency high because the wife's decision to leave or to resume her work is the pivot.
critical_reading: The film's framing treats Anjana's return to the stage as the provocation and Shekhar's absorption in work as ordinary, and the reconciliation is motivated by duty to his mother rather than by either of them conceding the argument. That said, it does let her keep the career, which many contemporaries would not have.

initial_relationship: Strangers thrown together by a road accident
how_they_meet: Sapna, having run away from her father in a red MG, collides with Sunil, who is working on his Jeep.
courtship_pattern: A journey rather than a courtship: he escorts her across the country toward the poet she is chasing, loving her the whole way without saying so to any effect.
emotional_dynamic: Warm companionship on her side, unreturned love on his, with the imbalance known to him alone.
pair_conflict: She is in love with an idea of a man she has never met, and Sunil is the one delivering her to him.
pair_friction_explanation: Comic scrapes and the friction of the road rather than genuine antagonism. The obstacle is not conflict between them but the fact that her attachment is elsewhere.
external_opposition_explanation: Sapna's father posts a reward that turns greedy strangers into pursuers, and has a psychiatrist pronounce her in need of confinement. The poet Ujjwala, whom she has met only through his verse, occupies the place Sunil wants.
lover_boy_explanation: Sunil's entire function is to love a woman who is pursuing someone else and to help her do it anyway. Devotion without return, sustained across the whole film and expressed through service rather than claim, is close to the centre of the archetype; it falls short of the top only because the film is a comedy and the feeling is largely unspoken.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The road-movie format gives Kapoor and Tagore more incidental playing than most of his 1970s pairings, and his unspoken attachment reads clearly against her preoccupation; the songs carry what the dialogue leaves unsaid.
actor_transformation: None recorded; Sunil's constancy is the fixed quantity.
female_transformation: Sapna moves from a literary infatuation toward the recognition the film's ending turns on.
relationship_outcome: Left at the denouement, where Sapna must reconcile the poet she loves with the man beside her.
relationship_analysis: One of the highest lover-boy scores in the early filmography attached to one of the lowest mutuality scores, which is the point: the role is built on devotion that is not returned for almost the entire running time. It anticipates the structure of Muqaddar Ka Sikandar-style unrequited devotion that the period's male stars increasingly took on.
critical_reading: Sapna's father has her declared in need of psychiatric confinement for an enthusiasm, which the film uses as comic pressure rather than examining; a modern reading finds the casual medicalising of a young woman's independence harder to pass over than the film intends. Sunil's decision to take her where she wants to go, rather than where he wants her, is the pairing's most creditable feature.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Raj Kumar, a musician in Nairobi, meets Sangeeta at a function and falls in love with her.
courtship_pattern: Not documented; the article's plot section is three sentences long.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented.
pair_conflict: Not documented. The only complication the summary records is that Rani Mehta also loves him.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is recorded anywhere in the sources consulted; the score reflects an attachment the summary presents as straightforward rather than any positive evidence of harmony.
external_opposition_explanation: Rani Mehta's love for Raj Kumar is the only obstacle the plot summary names, and it is not described as acting on the couple in any particular way.
lover_boy_explanation: The character is a musician who falls in love at a function and is loved by a second woman, which is the romantic-lead function, but with three sentences of plot there is no evidence of devotion, sacrifice or pursuit on which to base a higher score.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The Indian Express notice praised Kapoor's performance while calling the film lifeless, which suggests the pairing was not what carried it; the third Kapoor and Tagore film in a year, and the least regarded.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Not documented.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the attachment is explicitly stated, but the article gives three sentences of plot, so this row is close to the minimum at which a pairing can honestly be entered. Most categorical fields are marked unclear rather than guessed, and the confidence grade reflects that.
critical_reading: There is not enough documented material to support a contemporary or modern reading of the relationship. The only critical judgement located, the Indian Express notice, addresses the film rather than the pairing.

initial_relationship: A film star and the foreign author researching his industry
how_they_meet: Lucia, a British writer researching the Hindi film industry, meets Vikram in the course of that work.
courtship_pattern: An affair rather than a courtship, conducted around his marriage and under the eyes of a friend who wants her.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual attraction complicated on both sides, hers by what she is there to observe and his by a wife and a friend.
pair_conflict: Vikram is married, and Hari, his friend, is in love with Lucia.
pair_friction_explanation: The article's plot summary records complication rather than antagonism. The pressure on the pair comes from Vikram's marriage and Hari's feeling rather than from conflict between the two of them, but the position is unstable enough that it cannot be scored as frictionless.
external_opposition_explanation: Vikram's marriage stands directly against the affair, and Hari's love for Lucia makes the friendship a second obstacle. The cultural distance between a Hindi film star and a British author observing him is the film's wider subject.
lover_boy_explanation: Vikram is a star trading on his glamour rather than a man courting: the relationship is an affair he conducts alongside a marriage, with no devotion, sacrifice or constancy recorded. The role is about celebrity and its appetites rather than about love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor plays opposite his own wife, Jennifer Kendal, and the film exploits the real familiarity between them for a relationship that has to read as immediately intimate and fundamentally unserious.
actor_transformation: Not detailed by the article's brief plot summary.
female_transformation: Not detailed.
relationship_outcome: Not stated by the article's plot summary.
relationship_analysis: The second of the Merchant Ivory films in which Kapoor plays a charming man conducting two attachments at once, after Shakespeare Wallah; in both the woman is a foreigner observing India and in both he declines to choose. Casting his wife as the other woman in a film about a married film star adds a layer the production was plainly aware of.
critical_reading: The film is knowing about the exoticism it trades in, putting a British writer's fascination with a Hindi film star at the centre and letting the star be considerably less romantic than she has decided he is. What it does not examine is the wife, who exists in the plot summary only as the fact that complicates the affair.

actress_prominence: Female lead, one of two roles in a double part
initial_relationship: An army officer and the intruder caught stealing rations from his base
how_they_meet: Stranded by a Kashmir snowstorm with no food, Kamini sneaks into an army base, hears Captain Ajit reciting poetry, is caught stealing supplies and is chased down by him.
courtship_pattern: A single night: a chase, a rescue and an attraction both feel at once, ended by her leaving at dawn before he learns her name.
emotional_dynamic: Quick, high-spirited and mutual, then sustained for the rest of the film as a memory each believes lost.
pair_conflict: Nothing between them; the obstacle is that he does not know who she is and becomes engaged to her twin.
pair_friction_explanation: The chase and the theft are played as comic sparring rather than conflict, and once they are acquainted the pair are entirely aligned. What separates them is an identity problem, not a disagreement.
external_opposition_explanation: The twin sister and the marriage negotiated for her by Baba, Ajit's foster father, stand directly in the way, and the arrangement is made precisely because Ajit believes the Kashmir woman is lost to him. The opposition is structural and accidental rather than anyone's intention.
lover_boy_explanation: Ajit is introduced reciting poetry alone, falls in love in a night, and carries the attachment for the rest of the film as something he has given up for lost. That is the romantic register squarely, though the part is also a serving officer in a film with a suspense strand, which keeps it below the top band.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses the pairing specifically, though the film article credits Kapoor and Raakhee with powerful and promising performances. The Kashmir sequence is the film's best stretch and the attraction is played fast and lightly, which is what makes the subsequent mix-up land.
actor_transformation: Ajit goes from a solitary officer to a man carrying an attachment he cannot name or find.
female_transformation: Kamini returns from the trip to discover her sister engaged to the man she met.
relationship_outcome: The mistake is exposed when the sisters and Ajit are in a room together, and Kanchan's engagement is broken off.
relationship_analysis: The first of two rows for this film, both played by Raakhee. The Kamini relationship is the one the film treats as real, and it is unusually mutual for the period: she initiates as much as he does, and the separation is caused by an accident of information rather than by any family veto or class barrier.
critical_reading: The twin device lets the film have a heroine who is bold, mobile and sexually forward without making her the woman the hero was initially offered, and the resolution requires the shy sister to be set aside. Kamini's assertiveness is rewarded, but only after the narrative has used Kanchan's disappointment to make the point.

actress_prominence: Female lead, the second of two roles in a double part
initial_relationship: A prospective bride and groom introduced by his foster father
how_they_meet: Baba, Ajit's foster father, proposes Kanchan as a bride; Ajit sees her and takes her for the woman he met in Kashmir.
courtship_pattern: A formal arranged introduction that Ajit accepts with delight for the wrong reason, and that Kanchan accepts believing herself loved.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine happiness on her side resting entirely on his error, which neither of them can see.
pair_conflict: The engagement exists because Ajit has mistaken her for her twin, and it cannot survive the twin's return.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no antagonism between them at all; Kanchan is delighted and Ajit is willing. The damage is done by a misidentification rather than by conduct, and it is fatal to the engagement without either party quarrelling.
external_opposition_explanation: Kanchan's shyness has already cost her several matches, families having preferred her livelier sister, and the same sister is the reason this engagement collapses. The obstacle is her twin's existence.
lover_boy_explanation: Ajit is not courting Kanchan at all; he is agreeing to marry a woman he believes is someone else. There is no devotion directed at this person, which is precisely the film's cruelty, and the score reflects the absence of any romantic intention toward her.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Raakhee differentiates the two sisters clearly enough that the audience holds the mistake while the characters do not, and the Kanchan scenes are pitched deliberately flatter than the Kashmir ones.
actor_transformation: None toward Kanchan; Ajit's feeling was never hers to begin with.
female_transformation: Kanchan moves from a woman repeatedly passed over to one briefly and mistakenly chosen, and then passed over again.
relationship_outcome: The marriage is called off once Kamini returns and the misunderstanding is explained to Baba.
relationship_analysis: A second row is warranted because this is a distinct relationship with a distinct character, and it carries the film's real cost. The pair-friction score is low while the relationship-health score is among the lowest in the batch, which is the useful signal: harm here comes from a false premise, not from conflict.
critical_reading: The film is titled for Kanchan's shyness and then uses it to make her the sister who loses. Her repeated rejection by prospective families is presented sympathetically, but the plot's resolution endorses the same preference, delivering Ajit to the sister who was forward enough to break into an army base.

initial_relationship: Strangers on a train; she takes him for a thief
how_they_meet: Shyam meets Renu on a train to Dehradun and is drawn to her; she finds her purse in his coat and takes him for the thief, until it emerges that Kuldeep planted it.
courtship_pattern: An apology after a false accusation, then a growing closeness that he later sets about destroying on purpose.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual attachment, sabotaged from within by Shyam's decision that his benefactor's claim outranks his own.
pair_conflict: Shyam acts distant, urges Renu to marry Amar Singh, and finally drinks in order to repel her.
pair_friction_explanation: Substantial and deliberate, and unusually it is manufactured by Kapoor's own character: he withdraws, pushes her toward another man and stages his own degradation to make himself unacceptable. Renu resists throughout, so the conflict is entirely one-sided.
external_opposition_explanation: Chandan Singh is insulted at the suggestion that his sister marry a servant's son, and rivalry follows. Amar Singh's attachment to Renu, who resembles his dead sweetheart Kamla, and her family's wish that she marry him for their security both press against the couple.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is organised around renunciation for love, which is close to the centre of the archetype, though the renunciation is directed at a benefactor rather than at the woman's happiness. Devotion is expressed by giving her up, and the self-destruction is genuine.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The train meeting is the liveliest part of the pairing and the rest is played in a minor key as Kapoor withdraws; Vimi carries the second half, since Renu's refusal to be handed on is the only active resistance in the film.
actor_transformation: From an easy suitor to a man performing his own ruin, and back once Amar Singh releases him.
female_transformation: Renu refuses both her family's preference and Shyam's attempt to transfer her, holding to her own choice throughout.
relationship_outcome: Amar Singh learns what has been happening and unites them; they marry after Chandan Singh's attempt on his life fails.
relationship_analysis: A clear instance of the renunciation plot, in which the obstacle is the hero's own sense of obligation rather than anything external forbidding the match. Female agency scores high because Renu declines every arrangement made for her, by her family and by Shyam alike, which is rarer in this batch than the resolution suggests.
critical_reading: The film treats Shyam's attempt to hand Renu to his benefactor as nobility, and her refusal as devotion rather than as the obvious objection to being transferred between men as a debt payment. Amar Singh's attachment, rooted in Renu resembling her dead sister, is presented as poignant rather than as the substitution it is.

initial_relationship: Strangers divided by a killing between their fathers
how_they_meet: Shekhar meets Meena and both fall in love; the plot summary gives no circumstance.
courtship_pattern: Brief. The obstacle is raised and removed quickly, and the marriage takes place well before the midpoint.
emotional_dynamic: Settled and domestic once married, then increasingly strained by Shekhar's pursuit of the tiger.
pair_conflict: Shekhar's obsession with the man-eater, which takes him from the house and ends with him proposing to stake their son.
pair_friction_explanation: Low through the courtship and marriage, then sharply higher once Shekhar vows not to come home until the tiger is dead and finally resolves to use Raju as bait. The plot summary does not record Meena's response, but a father staking their infant is an interpersonal rupture of the first order.
external_opposition_explanation: Meena's father Gokuldas had killed Shekhar's father, so the marriage is barred by a killing until Gokuldas is himself killed by Mohan and the past is set aside. Thereafter the opposition is the animal rather than any person.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is settled early and the film is an animal-hunt adventure thereafter. Shekhar is a husband and then an obsessive; the courtship is perfunctory and the second half actively sets him against his own family, which is the opposite of the archetype.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The second of three Kapoor and Raakhee films in three years and the one that gives them least to do together, the marriage being largely a setup for the hunt; the pairing is warm but functional.
actor_transformation: From suitor to husband to a man whose fixation overrides his family.
female_transformation: Not recorded; Meena's position after the decision about Raju is not given by the summary.
relationship_outcome: Unresolved at the point the plot summary reaches, with Shekhar about to use their son as bait.
relationship_analysis: A marriage across a blood feud that is cleared away in a sentence so the film can get to the tiger. The interest for this project is the shape: romance resolved early and then progressively subordinated, with the husband's obsession replacing external opposition as the threat to the family. The same structure recurs in the action films of the following decade.
critical_reading: The feud is settled by a convenient third-party killing rather than by anything either partner does, and Meena has no recorded position on the decision that drives the climax, despite it concerning her child. The film's moral attention is on Shekhar's guilt about the animal he wounded rather than on what he is prepared to risk.

initial_relationship: A wandering ascetic and a celebrated courtesan
how_they_meet: Siddhartha, having left asceticism, comes to Kamala to be taught what he does not know.
courtship_pattern: Instruction rather than courtship: she teaches him pleasure and the conduct of the world, and he enters the merchant's life to be worth her time.
emotional_dynamic: Deliberately transactional at the outset and genuinely attached later, on both sides, without either pretending it is permanent.
pair_conflict: Siddhartha's search does not end with her, and the life he takes up to stay near her is the one he comes to loathe.
pair_friction_explanation: Little conflict between them; the relationship is clear-eyed on both sides about what it is. The rupture comes from Siddhartha's self-revulsion at the merchant's existence rather than from anything between him and Kamala.
external_opposition_explanation: No family, rival or social force acts against the pair. The only opposition is the philosophical one, that this way of living cannot be where Siddhartha's search ends.
lover_boy_explanation: The relationship is a stage in a spiritual progression rather than a romance the character is organised around. Siddhartha seeks Kamala out as an education in sensuality, and leaves when the lesson is exhausted; there is no devotion, pursuit or sacrifice for love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the American notices the article records address the film's solemnity rather than the performances. The playing is cool and formal by design, which suits a relationship framed as instruction, though it gives the pairing little warmth.
actor_transformation: Kamala moves Siddhartha from asceticism into the world of the senses and of money, which he must then exhaust and reject.
female_transformation: Not detailed by the sources consulted.
relationship_outcome: Siddhartha leaves the merchant's life and Kamala with it, continuing toward the equilibrium the film ends on.
relationship_analysis: The most unusual pairing in the filmography to this point: a courtesan who is the hero's teacher rather than his prize, in a relationship neither party treats as a destination. Female agency is scored the highest in the batch because Kamala sets the terms, owns her position and is never dependent on Siddhartha's choices.
critical_reading: The film inherits Hesse's framing, in which a woman's sexual expertise is an instrument of a European-facing spiritual narrative about an Indian man, and Kamala exists to be transcended. That said, she is granted a competence and self-possession that few women in Kapoor's mainstream films of the same years are given.

initial_relationship: Strangers on holiday; he teases her
how_they_meet: Preeti, a young doctor holidaying in Simla, meets Prem, an amateur skater, who teases her before falling for her.
courtship_pattern: Teasing into wooing into a proposal made immediately after they become intimate, all inside one holiday.
emotional_dynamic: Ardent and uncomplicated between the two of them, and then conducted for years entirely through what each believes the other did.
pair_conflict: None of their own. Every rupture is manufactured by Preeti's father, who forges Prem's letter into a demand for money.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple never quarrel. Preeti turns away because she is shown a forged letter, and Prem stays silent later to protect her engagement; the estrangement is total but the friction between them is almost nil, which is the defining shape of this pairing.
external_opposition_explanation: Heerachand tries to buy Prem off, forges his letter, arranges the birth away from Bombay, hands the newborn to Prem and tells his daughter the child was stillborn. It is among the most comprehensive paternal interventions in the filmography, and it separates the couple for years and costs Preeti her son.
lover_boy_explanation: Prem refuses the money, proposes at once, raises their son alone through polio, keeps silent about the forgery to protect Preeti's engagement to another man, and dies saving someone else's sister. Devotion, sacrifice and constancy are the whole content of the role; it falls short of the top only because the courtship is brief and the film's second half is a melodrama of concealment rather than of courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The Simla courtship is played lightly and quickly, which makes the long separation work; Kapoor and Tagore, by their fourth film together, handle the later scenes of suppressed recognition with more economy than the plot around them deserves.
actor_transformation: From a holiday flirt to a single father who conceals the truth even when telling it would restore him.
female_transformation: Preeti moves from a woman who believes she was sold, through mourning a child who is alive, to an attachment to her own son that she cannot account for.
relationship_outcome: Prem is mortally injured saving Amar's sister and hands over their son as he dies.
relationship_analysis: The highest external-opposition score in the batch paired with one of the lowest friction scores, and the clearest statement of the pattern that dominates Kapoor's romantic roles: the couple are never the problem, the father is. The film is also unusually explicit for 1973, turning on a pre-marital pregnancy and a child concealed from its mother.
critical_reading: The intimacy is framed as an accident of hypothermia and immediately converted into a proposal, which is how the period licensed the scene at all; the film then punishes Preeti with years of grief while treating Heerachand's forgery as paternal excess rather than as the theft of a child. Prem's long silence is presented as nobility, though it prolongs her loss for the sake of another man's engagement.

initial_relationship: A wealthy idler wooing a woman who wants none of it
how_they_meet: Not specified; Dilip spends much of his time wooing Leena, who rebuffs him before giving in.
courtship_pattern: Persistent pursuit against refusal, in the comic register, until she relents.
emotional_dynamic: Light and teasing in the first half, then subordinated entirely to Dilip's revenge once his parentage is revealed.
pair_conflict: Her initial refusal, and afterwards nothing; the film's conflict moves wholly to the revenge plot.
pair_friction_explanation: The rebuffs are comic and temporary and the couple are aligned once she accepts him. No serious interpersonal conflict is recorded, and Leena joins Dilip and Ram in the plan against Raghuveer.
external_opposition_explanation: Karamchand is arranging Dilip's marriage to his friend Poonamchand's daughter, which stands against Leena, and the revenge plot that takes over the film puts the pair in the path of Raghuveer and his men.
lover_boy_explanation: The wooing occupies much of the first half and is the character's main activity until the deathbed revelation, after which romance is displaced entirely by revenge. A romantic lead in the opening movement and something else thereafter.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The courtship is standard-issue for the period and the film's real interest is the friendship between Dilip and Ram; Leena is written into the revenge plan, which gives the pairing more to do than most subordinate romances of this batch.
actor_transformation: Dilip's transformation is from carefree heir to avenger, and it has nothing to do with Leena.
female_transformation: Leena moves from rebuffing him to joining his plan against Raghuveer.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the plot summary ends inside the revenge plot.
relationship_analysis: A courtship that exists to establish the hero's carefree life so that its destruction registers. Once Dilip learns who he is, the romance stops developing and Leena is converted into an accomplice, which is a common fate for the heroine in the revenge films that increasingly dominate this stretch of the filmography.
critical_reading: The persistence-against-refusal courtship is the period's default and the film does not examine it; Leena's initial rebuffs function as delay rather than as a position. Her later inclusion in the plan is a mild improvement on the pattern, giving her something to do besides wait.

initial_relationship: In love before the film's conflict begins
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Vijay, an engineer, is already in love with the wealthy Rekha when the plot starts.
courtship_pattern: Settled affection interrupted by a wrongful conviction, then resumed after his escape.
emotional_dynamic: Constant on both sides; neither wavers, and Rekha reconnects with him after the jailbreak rather than abandoning him.
pair_conflict: None between them. Every obstacle is imposed.
pair_friction_explanation: No interpersonal conflict is recorded at any point. The couple's alignment is total, which throws the entire dramatic weight onto the father and the politician.
external_opposition_explanation: Rekha's father objects to Vijay's lack of wealth, arranges her marriage to an evil politician's son, and then joins that politician in framing Vijay for a crime he did not commit, which puts him in prison. The opposition escalates from disapproval to manufactured conviction.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is a romantic hero in the masala register: wronged for loving above his station, constant throughout, and finally vindicated. It stops short of the top band because the second half turns him into a village's protector, and it is that public heroism rather than the courtship that changes her father's mind.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Mumtaz play an established couple rather than a developing one, and the warmth is easy and unforced; it was the film that made him one of the most saleable stars of the decade, and the pairing is a substantial part of why it worked.
actor_transformation: From a wronged man seeking to clear himself to one who chooses a village's safety over his own liberty.
female_transformation: Rekha holds to Vijay against her father's arrangement and reconnects with him after his escape.
relationship_outcome: Her father repents and accepts Vijay as his future son-in-law, with the prison sentences expected to be reduced.
relationship_analysis: The class romance in its fully commercial form, and the film that made Kapoor a top-rank star. Pair friction of one against external opposition of eight is the sharpest version of the split that characterises his whole romantic persona: he is never in conflict with the woman, only with her father, her class and the state.
critical_reading: The resolution requires Vijay to earn the father's approval through a public act of heroism rather than the father to abandon the objection, so the class barrier is satisfied rather than refuted. Rekha's constancy is genuine but she is not given a decisive action of her own; the men resolve the matter between them.
