initial_relationship: A crown prince and a poor young woman
how_they_meet: Ganga meets Jugni, who is from a poor family, and both fall in love and want to marry.
courtship_pattern: Brief and mutual, and then terminated not by the father's veto but by Ganga's abrupt change of character.
emotional_dynamic: Sincere and reciprocated until he becomes unrecognisable.
pair_conflict: Ganga turns womanising and drunken and agrees to marry the wealthy Mala instead, abandoning Jugni without explanation.
pair_friction_explanation: Low at first and then severe: the man Jugni loves becomes a different person and takes the match his father wanted. The plot summary withholds the reason, so the friction is scored on the conduct as presented.
external_opposition_explanation: Balbir Singh refuses to accept a poor daughter-in-law and intends Ganga for the wealthy Mala. Behind that stands the usurped throne and the murdered cousin, the concealed history that the character change appears to be connected to.
lover_boy_explanation: The role begins as a soft-spoken prince in love across class, which is the archetype, and then inverts into debauchery and an advantageous marriage. Scored at the midpoint because the film contains both the romantic hero and his repudiation, with the summary not explaining which is the real one.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The fifth Kapoor and Tagore pairing in five years; the early scenes rely on that established familiarity, and the interest of the performance is in the reversal rather than in the courtship.
actor_transformation: A reversal rather than a development: from fair-minded and soft-spoken to womanising, alcoholic and foul-mouthed.
female_transformation: Not recorded; the summary leaves Jugni heartbroken and asks what she will do.
relationship_outcome: Abandoned, with Ganga willing to wed Mala; the summary stops before any resolution.
relationship_analysis: A class romance that is broken not by the father who opposes it but by the man inside it, for reasons the plot summary deliberately withholds. Kapoor plays a dual role here, and given that the coup which opens the film kills a twin, the character change may well be an impersonation rather than a corruption, but no source consulted confirms it.
critical_reading: Jugni is given no agency in her own abandonment and the summary's closing question, what the poor heart-broken Jugni will do now, positions her as a spectator of the men's plot. The wealthy Mala is similarly a counter rather than a character, and the film's interest is in the dynastic puzzle rather than in either woman.

actress_prominence: Female lead of the film, opposite Manoj Kumar
initial_relationship: Employer and secretary; she is another man's girlfriend
how_they_meet: Sheetal takes work as secretary to the rich businessman Mohan Babu, and he becomes attracted to her.
courtship_pattern: Proximity at work, then a straightforward proposal of marriage made at the point where her patience with Bharat's poverty has run out.
emotional_dynamic: Attraction on his side and a clear-eyed calculation on hers; she loves Bharat and cannot contemplate a life in poverty with him.
pair_conflict: Sheetal does not love Mohan, and the marriage is a decision about money rather than about him.
pair_friction_explanation: No antagonism between them and no quarrel recorded. The unease is structural: the relationship rests on an economic choice she later regrets, and Mohan is not the object of the regret.
external_opposition_explanation: Bharat's prior claim is the standing obstacle, though it works against him only in Sheetal's conscience. Mohan's wealth is what makes the match possible rather than what obstructs it, which reverses the usual arrangement in Kapoor's romances.
lover_boy_explanation: Mohan wins a woman by being able to afford her, in a film whose argument is about what poverty costs. He is decent rather than predatory, but there is no courtship, devotion or sacrifice, and he functions as the economic alternative rather than as a romantic figure.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film keeps Kapoor and Zeenat Aman deliberately cool together, since the audience is meant to feel the absence of what she had with Bharat; the restraint is correct for the part but leaves the pairing muted.
actor_transformation: Little. Mohan ends the film fighting alongside Bharat and the others against Nekiram.
female_transformation: Sheetal chooses wealth over love, regrets it, and finally sacrifices her life in the conflict with Nekiram.
relationship_outcome: Ends with Sheetal's death; Bharat marries Tulsi, in whom he sees her.
relationship_analysis: A pairing row is warranted because the marriage is real and consequential, but the position is unusual in the filmography: Kapoor is the man the heroine settles for rather than the one she is kept from. Mutuality is scored low and female agency relatively high for the same reason, that Sheetal's choice is deliberate, informed and hers.
critical_reading: The film's moral scheme punishes Sheetal for choosing security over love, killing her and then having Bharat find her replacement in a poorer, more devoted woman. Mohan, who did nothing worse than propose, is treated far more leniently than the woman who accepted, which is the period's usual distribution of blame.

initial_relationship: Sweethearts, both trapped by poverty
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; they are sweethearts when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: No courtship. The relationship exists from the outset and the film is about what money does to it.
emotional_dynamic: Attachment under continuous economic pressure, with both of them carrying family obligations that leave nothing over.
pair_conflict: Not conflict so much as parallel corruption: a job in a wealthy world costs both of them their moral compass.
pair_friction_explanation: The article's four-sentence summary records no quarrel, but states that both parties lose their bearings, which implies damage to the relationship without specifying its form. Scored at the midpoint and graded low confidence accordingly.
external_opposition_explanation: Extreme poverty on both sides: Raj must provide for his family and fund his sister's wedding, while Poonam nurses an ailing mother on pennies and her father drinks his earnings. The wealthy world Raj enters for work is the corrupting force.
lover_boy_explanation: The pairing is the film's emotional centre, but the role is defined by economic compulsion rather than by courtship or devotion, and the character loses his moral compass rather than proving himself through constancy.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The sixth Kapoor and Tagore film, and by this point the pairing carries an accumulated familiarity that a four-sentence plot cannot really test; the film underperformed and little was written about it.
actor_transformation: From a poor man with intact principles to one whose bearings are gone.
female_transformation: Poonam undergoes the same loss in parallel, according to the article's summary.
relationship_outcome: Not stated by the article's plot summary.
relationship_analysis: Included because the sweetheart relationship is explicitly stated and is the frame for the whole plot, but the article gives four sentences and the film was a commercial failure that attracted little writing, so several fields are marked unclear. The premise, that poverty corrupts both partners rather than ennobling them, is notably bleaker than the class romances around it.
critical_reading: Too little of the film is documented to support a developed reading. What is recorded is unusual for its moment in refusing to make poverty morally improving, and in applying the corruption to the woman as well as the man.

initial_relationship: A jobless graduate and the daughter of a Deputy Commissioner of Police
how_they_meet: Not dramatised in detail; Ravi romances Veera, the daughter of DCP Narang, while unable to find work.
courtship_pattern: A light courtship threaded between the film's major scenes, with her father sponsoring Ravi's police training.
emotional_dynamic: Uncomplicated and supportive, functioning as relief from the fraternal tragedy rather than as a story of its own.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict of any kind is recorded between Ravi and Veera. The relationship is entirely harmonious and exists outside the film's lines of tension, which all run between the brothers and their mother.
external_opposition_explanation: Almost none. Veera's father is not an obstacle but a patron, sending Ravi for police training; the class difference between a slum-raised graduate and a DCP's daughter is never made into a barrier.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is a minor thread in a film about two brothers, a mother and the law. Ravi's identity is organised around duty and his relationship with Vijay; Veera is a companion rather than a motivation, and none of the character's defining choices concern her.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; the reviews located praise Kapoor's performance and the film at large rather than this pairing. Kapoor and Neetu Singh are pleasant and unforced together, and the scenes function as designed, as air between the heavy fraternal confrontations.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: Intact. Veera is present with Ravi and his mother at the awarding that closes the film.
relationship_analysis: The clearest case in the filmography of a romance that exists because the format requires one. In the film that won Kapoor his Filmfare award and gave him his most quoted line, the romance scores three for centrality and one for friction, and nothing about the character's arc runs through it. It is the template for his 1970s multi-starrer romances.
critical_reading: Veera is written without a stake in anything the film is about; she is present at the beginning of Ravi's career and at its vindication, and absent from every decision in between. The film's emotional weight is given entirely to the mother, which is a recurring feature of the Salim-Javed scripts of this period.

initial_relationship: Newly married, by an arrangement he entered in good faith
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Dheeraj's bride is revealed to be Kamini, the woman his best friend Rajesh had renounced.
who_initiates: Not recorded; the marriage is arranged
courtship_pattern: No courtship is shown. The marriage exists before the audience learns whom he has married.
emotional_dynamic: Dheeraj is affectionate and unsuspecting; Kamini is hostile to Rajesh and dutiful to her husband, carrying a renunciation Dheeraj knows nothing about.
pair_conflict: A police file asserting that Kamini and Rajesh love each other, which Dheeraj reads and cannot un-read.
pair_friction_explanation: Severe once the file surfaces: Dheeraj drinks, confronts them both and accuses Rajesh of romancing his wife. The mistrust is substantial and directed at Kamini as much as at his friend, even though she has done nothing since the marriage.
external_opposition_source: Existing relationship; War or politics; Crime
external_opposition_explanation: Rajesh's prior claim, renounced to spare her widowhood, sits inside the marriage from the start. Around it are the independence struggle, Dheeraj's position as a colonial police officer sheltering a wanted revolutionary, a constable seeking promotion by exposing them, and Sher Khan's torture and suicide.
lover_boy_explanation: Dheeraj is a husband and a friend rather than a lover: there is no courtship, and his defining acts are protecting Rajesh and then accusing him. The film's romantic ache belongs to Rajesh Khanna's poet, and Kapoor plays the man who holds the position the lover gave up.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film gives Kapoor and Mumtaz little to play as a couple, since the charge runs between her and Rajesh Khanna; what Kapoor supplies is the decency that makes the triangle painful rather than sordid.
actor_transformation: From an untroubled husband and friend to a man who accuses them both and then saves Rajesh from the police anyway.
female_transformation: Kamini moves from hostility toward the man who abandoned her to shooting him in order to protect her husband.
relationship_outcome: Kamini shoots Rajesh when he points a gun at Dheeraj and declares he means to take her; the marriage stands.
relationship_analysis: The second film in this batch, after Kabhi Kabhie's shape, in which Kapoor plays the husband rather than the lover, and the pattern is becoming a type: he is the decent man occupying a place another man vacated, and his dramatic function is to be generous and then to doubt. Kamini's final act, shooting the poet to protect the husband, is the strongest female action in the batch.
critical_reading: Rajesh's renunciation, undertaken to spare Kamini the cruelties of widowhood, disposes of her future without consulting her, and the film presents it as sacrifice rather than presumption. Her hostility toward him is the most reasonable position anyone in the film holds, and the plot rewards it by making her the one who must fire.

initial_relationship: Inseparable childhood neighbours, parted when his father is arrested
how_they_meet: They are childhood friends and neighbours; years later they meet again as adults under different names, neither recognising the other.
courtship_pattern: A second courtship between two people who were once inseparable and do not know it, each living under an assumed name.
emotional_dynamic: Immediate mutual attraction carrying an unrecognised history underneath it.
pair_conflict: Both are living false identities, and he is travelling to her birthplace to have himself jailed for a gangster's fee.
pair_friction_explanation: No antagonism between them is recorded. The instability is in the concealment on both sides rather than in conflict, and the article's plot summary ends before the recognition forces anything.
external_opposition_explanation: His father's arrest for burglary separated them as children and set his own course as a thief. The gangster's commission that takes him toward jail, and the separate lives and names they have built, are the standing obstacles.
lover_boy_explanation: A romantic lead in a crime picture: the attachment is genuine and gives the character his only reason to leave the criminal errand, but the role is a card sharp and thief first, and the film's second half is a jail plot rather than a courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The reunion-without-recognition premise gives the pairing a built-in warmth that the playing does not have to manufacture; Sulakshana Pandit, primarily a singer, is given a performer's role that suits her.
actor_transformation: Begun rather than completed: Seema gives the thief a reason to abandon the commission he is travelling to fulfil.
female_transformation: Guddi becomes Seema, a professional stage singer and dancer, and is travelling to her birthplace on a religious errand when they meet.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the article's plot summary ends with both journeys still in progress.
relationship_analysis: The childhood-separation-and-reunion device, common in the period's family melodramas, applied to a romance rather than to siblings. Both halves of the couple have changed names and classes, which makes the mutual non-recognition symmetrical, unusual in a filmography where the concealed identity is normally the man's alone.
critical_reading: The film's symmetry is its most modern feature: Seema is not waiting to be discovered but has built a career and a name of her own, and the recognition when it comes will cost her as much as him. The plot summary does not reach the point where either has to answer for the concealment.

initial_relationship: A gang leader and a young woman, an attachment the film calls unexpected
how_they_meet: Not specified; Ajit, a notorious gang leader, unexpectedly falls in love with Sonali.
courtship_pattern: Not documented beyond the fact of the attachment.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented; the summary records the attachment and then its interruption.
pair_conflict: None between them. They are separated by an assassination attempt and a false report of his death.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is recorded. What ends the relationship is Sonali's reasonable belief that Ajit is dead, not anything either does to the other.
external_opposition_explanation: An enemy attempts to kill Ajit, and the belief that the attempt succeeded is what leads Sonali to marry another man. The criminal world he belongs to is the direct cause of the separation.
lover_boy_explanation: The attachment is presented as the one unexpected thing about a hardened gang leader, which gives the role a romantic dimension, but the film's second movement is revenge rather than love, and the summary records no attempt to recover her.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the article gives four sentences of plot with no character mappings in its cast list. The score is a low-confidence default reflecting the absence of any evidence either way.
actor_transformation: From a gangster softened by an unlikely attachment to one returning for revenge once it is gone.
female_transformation: Sonali believes Ajit dead and marries another man.
relationship_outcome: Lost. She is married to someone else when he returns, and he turns to revenge instead.
relationship_analysis: A thin row, entered because the attachment and its loss are both explicitly stated and are the engine of the plot. The identification of the actress rests on billing order rather than on a sourced character mapping, which is recorded in the film's research notes and reflected in the confidence grade.
critical_reading: Too little is documented for a developed reading. The structure, a woman who remarries in good faith and is then found by the returning man she mourned, is a standard of the period and usually resolved at her expense; this summary does not say how it resolves here.

initial_relationship: In love and intending to marry when the plot reaches them
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Geeta confides to her sister-in-law that she has met Ranjeet and that they love each other and want to marry.
courtship_pattern: Settled before the film addresses it; the drama is entirely in the opposition that follows.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and approved by her family, then driven apart by his father's ultimatum and his subsequent destitution.
pair_conflict: None between them. Ranjeet refuses the match his father demands and is disinherited for it.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple are aligned throughout and no quarrel is recorded. What separates them is his father's ultimatum and the poverty that follows it, together with the catastrophe that overtakes her household while she is away.
external_opposition_explanation: Mayadas orders Ranjeet to marry a wealthy man's daughter and throws him out when he refuses. In parallel Geeta's own family collapses: her brother is persuaded by his wife to abandon their parents and the loans, her father dies, and her mother is blinded in a fire while she is in Paris.
lover_boy_explanation: Ranjeet gives up an inheritance rather than marry the woman his father has chosen, which is rebellion for love and the core of the archetype. The score is held below the top band because the film's weight is on Geeta and her parents, and because his destitution turns him toward crime rather than toward pursuit.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The third Kapoor and Hema Malini film in this batch; the courtship is largely offscreen and the two are given more to play in adversity than in affection.
actor_transformation: From a wealthy man's son who chooses love over an inheritance to a deadbeat contemplating crime to stay alive.
female_transformation: Geeta returns from three weeks abroad to a dead father, a blinded mother and a destitute fiance, having been the family's support throughout.
relationship_outcome: Not resolved at the point the article's plot summary reaches.
relationship_analysis: The disinheritance plot in its straightforward form, and notable for making the sacrifice costly rather than symbolic: Ranjeet refuses the arranged marriage and the film then shows him reduced to considering crime, instead of restoring him. Geeta is the family's earner throughout, which gives her a standing the romance itself does not.
critical_reading: The film's sympathy is with the children who support their parents and against the son who abandons them, and the romance is subordinate to that argument. Geeta's labour is what sustains the household before and after, but her three weeks in Paris are positioned as the interval during which everything goes wrong, which sits awkwardly with the film's own approval of her career.

initial_relationship: An arranged marriage made against the bride's wishes
how_they_meet: Pooja's parents arrange her marriage to Vijay, an architect, against her wishes and while she is in love with the poet Amit.
courtship_pattern: None. The marriage is the starting point, and the relationship is built over twenty years of ordinary life.
emotional_dynamic: Affectionate, comfortable and materially settled, resting on a foundation Vijay does not know the shape of.
pair_conflict: Pooja's first attachment, which surfaces when she introduces Amit on her television programme and Vijay begins to work out what he is looking at.
pair_friction_explanation: Two decades of harmony disturbed by a recognition rather than a quarrel. Vijay does not accuse Pooja; his anger, when it comes, is directed at Amit, and the discomfort between husband and wife is unspoken.
external_opposition_explanation: Amit's prior claim is inside the marriage from the wedding night, when Vijay unknowingly gives Pooja his rival's book of poems. The parents who arranged the match over her objection created the situation, and the second generation's crisis over Pinky's parentage brings both couples together again.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay is a husband, not a suitor: no courtship, no pursuit, no rebellion. He is generous, admiring of his wife's first love without knowing it, and eventually wounded. The film's lover-boy is Amit, and Kapoor plays the man who benefited from that romance failing.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Raakhee, in their fourth film together, play twenty years of marriage with an ease that makes the arrangement look chosen, which is what the film needs if Vijay's late discovery is to land.
actor_transformation: From an untroubled husband to one who understands what his marriage was built on, and decides to go on with it.
female_transformation: Pooja moves from a young woman married against her wishes to a public figure who introduces her first love to an audience, and back into the marriage.
relationship_outcome: The marriage holds through the reappearance of Amit and the crisis over Pinky's parentage.
relationship_analysis: The exact inversion of Jab Jab Phool Khile: there Kapoor is the man a woman defies her father to take, here the man a father hands her to over her objection. The film is unusual in Hindi cinema for staying with the arranged marriage rather than dissolving it, and for making the husband sympathetic enough that the audience does not want it dissolved.
critical_reading: The film's generosity to Vijay is real but it is also how it avoids its own question: Pooja was married against her wishes, and the resolution asks her to be content rather than asking whether the marriage should have been made. The wedding-night gift of Amit's poems is the sharpest image in the filmography of a woman handed her own loss by a man who means it kindly.

initial_relationship: A gang leader and the policewoman who has infiltrated his gang
how_they_meet: Neeta, a police officer, goes undercover into the criminal group Vijay runs as Fakira.
courtship_pattern: A courtship conducted entirely inside an operation, with the woman holding the deception rather than the man.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine attachment on both sides, undercut by her purpose and by a second woman's suspicion of her.
pair_conflict: She is there to destroy his organisation, and Neelam is working to expose her.
pair_friction_explanation: The deception is structural and irreducible: every scene between them is an operation for her. The article records no quarrel, but a relationship in which one partner is an undercover officer cannot be scored as low-friction.
external_opposition_explanation: Neelam loves Vijay and distrusts Neeta on that account, working against her inside the gang. Around them are Vijay's criminal position, the brother-enemy Toofan, and Chiman Lal.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance softens a criminal and gives the film its emotional line, but Vijay's identity is organised around the gang and the unrecognised brother rather than around courtship. He is a romantic lead in an action picture, not a devotee.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Shabana Azmi, a year into a career built on parallel cinema, plays the undercover officer with more reserve than the genre expects, which gives the attachment an ambiguity the writing does not supply.
actor_transformation: Not stated by the article's plot summary.
female_transformation: Not stated; the summary does not record whether Neeta completes her assignment.
relationship_outcome: Not stated by the article's plot summary.
relationship_analysis: Unusual in the filmography for putting the deception on the woman's side: Kapoor's characters routinely conceal an identity from the heroine, and here a policewoman conceals hers from him. Female agency is scored high because Neeta drives the plot rather than reacting to it, which is rare in his commercial films of this decade.
critical_reading: The undercover premise gives the heroine a profession and a purpose, but the film routes the tension through a second woman's jealousy rather than through the moral problem of the deception itself. Neelam's distrust of Neeta is correct on the facts and is nonetheless framed as possessiveness.

initial_relationship: An established attachment; the article calls her his sweetheart
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Sheila is Ravi's sweetheart when the plot begins.
courtship_pattern: No courtship is shown. The relationship exists to give the murder plot something to threaten.
emotional_dynamic: Not developed; the storyline records the attachment and then puts her in danger.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict is recorded between Ravi and Sheila anywhere in the article's storyline section. The score reflects the absence of friction in a relationship the film does not examine.
external_opposition_explanation: Swami Hari Om, the fraudulent godman Ravi's film was made to expose, discovers he is alive and abducts both his mother and Sheila, which is the crisis the storyline ends on.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi is a film star running from a murder charge, and the romance is a hostage rather than a pursuit. There is no courtship, devotion or sacrifice recorded; the relationship functions as leverage against him.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The first of five Kapoor and Rekha films in three years, and the one that gives them least to play, since the storyline keeps Sheila offscreen until she is taken.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the storyline ends with Sheila and Ravi's mother abducted.
relationship_analysis: A clear instance of the heroine-as-hostage pattern that recurs through Kapoor's action films of the late 1970s: the romance is established in a phrase, and its only narrative function is to be seized by the villain in the third act. Female agency is scored accordingly.
critical_reading: The film gives Sheila no part in its own plot beyond being taken, and pairs her abduction with the hero's mother's, which is precisely how the period's masala cinema ranks the women around its protagonist.

initial_relationship: Married with a young daughter when the film opens
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; they are married at the point of his conviction.
courtship_pattern: No courtship. The relationship is a marriage being dismantled by a criminal sentence and then reopened fourteen years later.
emotional_dynamic: Loyalty surviving a conviction, a presumed execution, a second marriage and fourteen years.
pair_conflict: He instructs her to take their daughter and start again, and then reappears alive into the life she built on that instruction.
pair_friction_explanation: Not antagonism but an impossible position, and one he creates twice: first by telling her to go, then by coming to Bombay. The friction is in the situation rather than in anything either says, and the summary records no quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: A conviction for molestation and murder, a death sentence upheld through two appeals and then commuted without her knowledge, fourteen years of separation, and Seema's second marriage to Ratan, whom she befriended and married in good faith.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is a husband and a convict, not a suitor. Its romantic content is renunciation, deciding not to disturb a family that appears happy, which is devotion of a kind but is expressed entirely as withdrawal.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film keeps the couple apart for most of its length, so what registers is not chemistry in the ordinary sense but the weight of the reunion, which Kapoor and Vidya Sinha play with restraint.
actor_transformation: From a condemned man giving instructions to his wife to one who decides his existence would only damage her.
female_transformation: Seema rebuilds a life by sewing, remarries, raises their daughter, and then seeks out the husband she believed executed.
relationship_outcome: Her secret visit to him sets off the chain of events the summary says changes all their lives.
relationship_analysis: A marriage examined across a fourteen-year gap and a bigamous situation neither partner created, and one of the few pairings in the filmography where the obstacle is the legal system rather than a father or a villain. It belongs with The Householder and Abhinetri in the group where Kapoor plays a husband and the drama is domestic.
critical_reading: The film's sympathy is with the husband's restraint, while Seema is the one who actually bore the consequences, raising a child alone on piecework before remarrying. That she is the one who breaks the impasse by seeking him out is the most interesting decision in the plot, and the summary treats it as the trigger for the men's crisis rather than as hers.

initial_relationship: Lovers, before the film's present action
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the relationship predates the story and is ended by his death.
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The relationship exists in Nisha's memory and in the resemblance she finds in another man.
emotional_dynamic: An attachment strong enough that its loss makes her a recluse and its echo in a stranger reopens everything.
pair_conflict: None recorded; the relationship is ended by death rather than by conflict.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is recorded. What the film examines is the aftermath of the relationship rather than the relationship, and nothing in it suggests discord.
external_opposition_explanation: Shashi Saigal's death, described as tragic, is the whole of the opposition and it is absolute. Everything the film contains happens because of it.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor's presence is a cameo and the character is dead before the action, so there is no courtship or devotion to score. He is scored at the midpoint because the entire film is organised around his having been loved, which is the archetype's afterlife rather than its performance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the part is a cameo with limited screen time. What the film requires is that the audience accept the attachment as formative for Nisha, which the casting of an established star in a brief role efficiently supplies.
actor_transformation: None; the character is fixed in the past.
female_transformation: Nisha moves from seclusion after his death to taking work with a man who reminds her of him, which is where the film's actual problem begins.
relationship_outcome: Ended by his death before the film's present action.
relationship_analysis: Included because the relationship is the film's premise rather than a detail: Doosra Aadmi, meaning the second man, is about a woman seeing a dead lover in a living one. The row records a relationship with far more narrative weight than Kapoor's screen time, which is precisely the distinction between billing and importance this project is built to track.
critical_reading: The film is unusually interested in a woman's grief as an active force rather than a state to be cured by a new man, and Nisha's pursuit of Karan is treated as a problem she creates rather than a reward she is owed. Kapoor's character, being dead, is idealised by construction, which is the point.

initial_relationship: Former college acquaintances; she is married to another man
how_they_meet: Vinod is hired by Aarti's sister to decorate the Khandala bungalow where Aarti is staying alone, and she remembers him from college.
courtship_pattern: Not courtship but pursuit: he spends time with her on the strength of the old acquaintance, establishes that she is unaccompanied, and presses himself on her.
emotional_dynamic: Familiarity exploited into threat, ending in a physical struggle.
pair_conflict: He will not accept refusal from a married woman who is alone, and she kills him resisting.
pair_friction_explanation: The highest friction score in the filmography to this point, and it is not a quarrel: the relationship is a pursuit the woman ends by killing the man. The article describes an intense scuffle in which Aarti accidentally kills Vinod, which places the pairing at the destructive end of the scale.
external_opposition_explanation: Aarti's marriage to Dr. Sunil Gupta is the standing fact Vinod is working against, and it is also, through his medical care of the amnesiac Vinod, what brings the threat back into the house.
lover_boy_explanation: The opposite of the archetype. There is no courtship, devotion or sacrifice; the character identifies a woman's isolation as an opportunity and acts on it. Scored at the floor of the scale rather than zero only because the film frames his interest as attraction rather than pure predation.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, though Raakhee was nominated for the Filmfare Best Actress award for the film. What the pairing requires is menace rather than warmth, and casting an actor with Kapoor's established romantic image as the predator is the film's sharpest decision.
actor_transformation: From an old college acquaintance to an assailant to an amnesiac whose recovery threatens the women who buried him.
female_transformation: Aarti moves from a lonely, childless wife to a woman who has killed her assailant and must conceal it, and then live with his return.
relationship_outcome: She kills him; he survives without memory and is brought back into her home by her own husband.
relationship_analysis: The single most important row in this batch for the project's analytical purpose. Kapoor's romantic persona is built on being the safe, courteous suitor, and Trishna inverts it completely: the same charm is used to isolate a married woman, and the film gives her the killing rather than a rescue. The scores invert with it, with friction at nine and lover-boy at one.
critical_reading: The film's own framing calls the death accidental and makes the women's concealment the source of suspense, which places the audience's anxiety with the killer rather than with the victim. By a modern reading that is the correct sympathy, and the film arrives at it almost in spite of its thriller mechanics: Aarti is defending herself in her own house, and the plot's threat is that her assailant will remember.

initial_relationship: A village priest's daughter and the engineer posted to build the dam
how_they_meet: Rajeev hears Roopa singing hymns at the village temple and meets her without seeing the burned right side of her face, which she keeps behind her sari.
courtship_pattern: A courtship conducted on a partial view: he falls in love with a voice and a half-seen face, and asks her father for her before he has seen her whole.
emotional_dynamic: Adoration on his side resting on a misapprehension, and love on hers compromised by the knowledge that he has not seen what he is marrying.
pair_conflict: He discovers the scarring after the wedding, decides he has been cheated, disowns her, and then takes a veiled mistress who is the same woman.
pair_friction_explanation: Severe and sustained damage originating entirely between the couple: he drives her out on the wedding night, ignores her by day while loving her disguised by night, accuses her of infidelity when she becomes pregnant by him, and shames her publicly. Her father dies of the disgrace.
external_opposition_explanation: The childhood accident that scarred her, the village's pressure on her to accept the proposal despite her own misgivings, and her father's complicity in not disclosing the scarring. The obstacles set the trap but the cruelty is Rajeev's own.
lover_boy_explanation: The film is a romance and Rajeev's pursuit drives the first act, so the romantic apparatus is fully present, but what the character actually does is reject, conceal and accuse. Scored at the midpoint because the role is a romantic lead in form and its opposite in conduct.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film's charge is in Zeenat Aman's performance and Raj Kapoor's photography of her rather than in the couple, and Kapoor's Rajeev is written to be withholding, so the pairing is deliberately unequal on screen as well as in the plot.
actor_transformation: From a man who cannot tolerate ugliness to one confronted with having loved, rejected, and impregnated the same woman without recognising her.
female_transformation: Roopa moves from concealment to a marriage she warned against, through rejection and a double life as her own husband's mistress, to a vow never to return to him on those terms.
relationship_outcome: Unresolved at the point of the storm, with the identity of wife and mistress collapsing together.
relationship_analysis: The lowest relationship-health score in the filmography so far, in a film with the highest possible romance centrality. It is also the clearest case of the distinction this project insists on between a film being about a relationship and that relationship being healthy: Satyam Shivam Sundaram is entirely about a marriage, and the marriage is an atrocity.
critical_reading: The film presents Rajeev's inability to see his wife as a spiritual failing to be corrected, and asks the audience to want the marriage restored. A modern reading finds a husband who evicts his disfigured wife, keeps her as a veiled mistress, and publicly accuses her of adultery over his own child; the film's celebrated aesthetic of the beautiful suffering woman is itself part of what it fails to examine, and its article carries a controversy section on that ground.

initial_relationship: Fellow workers at the same factory
how_they_meet: They work together at the factory making lead shielding containers; the article identifies her as a fellow worker and his love interest.
courtship_pattern: Not dramatised in the article's account; the relationship is established as a fact and then pays off when she saves him from the police.
emotional_dynamic: A working partnership that is also an attachment, with her taking the active role at the crisis.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair appears anywhere in the article's plot account. Their scenes are cooperative, and her decisive act in the film is on his behalf.
external_opposition_explanation: Heeralal's gang, which destroyed Laxman's family and now wants the uranium shielding his factory produces, and the police pursuit from which Rekha extracts him.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is a secondary thread in a film about three separated brothers and a smuggling ring. Laxman is defined by his work and his family history rather than by courtship, and the relationship is stated more than shown.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The relationship is given little screen time in an unusually crowded plot, but it is written as a partnership between equals at the same workplace, which is rarer in this filmography than its brevity suggests.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: None recorded, though she acts decisively in saving him from arrest.
relationship_outcome: Not separately resolved; the plot summary ends inside the convergence on Heeralal.
relationship_analysis: A minor romance, but worth recording for one feature: the woman and the man are colleagues at the same factory and she is the one who acts at the decisive moment. Against the batch's dominant patterns, hostage heroines and fathers with vetoes, a working partnership with no class gap and no paternal objection stands out.
critical_reading: The relationship is too briefly drawn to carry much reading, but its shape is notable in a film whose other romance, the brother Ram's pursuit of Kusum, begins as a deliberate deception to steal from her father and is then converted into love.

initial_relationship: Established: she is his girlfriend when he returns from abroad
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Sheetal, daughter and general manager of P. L. Verma, is already Shekhar's girlfriend.
courtship_pattern: No courtship. The relationship is settled and is then used as an instrument by a third party.
emotional_dynamic: Comfortable and largely untested until Vijay begins working on it deliberately.
pair_conflict: Vijay sets out to create differences between them as part of his campaign against the family.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple have no quarrel of their own. Such strain as develops is manufactured by Vijay for commercial leverage, and the article records the attempt rather than a rupture.
external_opposition_explanation: Vijay's campaign against the Gupta family, which includes deliberately trying to divide Shekhar and Sheetal, and the business rivalry between her father's company and both sides.
lover_boy_explanation: Shekhar is a businessman inside a revenge plot; the romance is settled before the film starts and never becomes his motivation. Nothing he does in the film is done for Sheetal, and the emotional weight of Trishul is entirely fraternal and paternal.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Hema Malini's Sheetal is written as a company's general manager rather than a decorative fiancee, which gives the pairing a professional register, but the film's real energy is between Bachchan, Sanjeev Kumar and Kapoor.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: None recorded; Sheetal holds her position through Vijay's attempt to exploit it.
relationship_outcome: Survives Vijay's interference; the family is reconciled by the end.
relationship_analysis: Another instance of the pattern that defines Kapoor's multi-starrer roles: the romance is pre-settled, low-friction and outside the film's argument, which is about a father's betrayal and an illegitimate son's revenge. Sheetal's standing as a working general manager gives the female-agency score a lift the plot function does not.
critical_reading: Sheetal is one of the few women in the batch with a named professional role, and the film still uses her chiefly as a pressure point between two men. That Vijay's tactic is to come between her and Shekhar, rather than to approach her on her own terms, is the clearest indication of how the script ranks her.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Heeralal meets Ruby and falls in love with her; the plot summary gives no circumstance.
courtship_pattern: Brief and uncontested, running in parallel with Pannalal's courtship of Ruby's friend Neelam.
emotional_dynamic: Light and companionable, pitched to match the film's comic register.
pair_conflict: None recorded.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is recorded at any point. The obstacles in the film are Kalicharan and Panther, and the couples are united at the end without any difficulty between them.
external_opposition_explanation: Kalicharan, who set out to punish Heeralal and Pannalal for interfering in his business and who turns out to have murdered Heeralal's parents, together with his associate Panther.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is one of two parallel courtships in a buddy action comedy, and Heeralal's driving motivation is the search for his parents' killer rather than Ruby. Pleasant rather than devotional.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The third Kapoor and Zeenat Aman film in four years; the double-couple structure gives each pairing limited room, and the film's interest is in the Heeralal and Pannalal partnership.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: Heeralal and Ruby are united, as are Pannalal and Neelam.
relationship_analysis: A paired-couples comedy in which the romances exist to be resolved in the last minute alongside the revenge plot. Its value for the project is mainly as another data point in the late-1970s pattern: near-zero pair friction, moderate villain-sourced opposition, and a romance that is never the character's motivation.
critical_reading: Ruby and Neelam are written as a matched pair for a matched pair of heroes, with no separate existence from that symmetry, which is the standard construction of the period's double-hero comedies.

initial_relationship: A village woman and the new police inspector
how_they_meet: Sandhya is a village belle in the posting Gautam is sent to, and comes to know him as he takes on the local power.
who_initiates: Sandhya, whose respect for him develops into love before he reciprocates
courtship_pattern: Gradual: respect earned through his conduct in the village, then affection, then reciprocation.
emotional_dynamic: Admiration maturing into attachment on her side, answered in time on his.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict is recorded between Gautam and Sandhya. The relationship develops steadily and she is his ally throughout, including at the point where she intervenes to save him.
external_opposition_explanation: Dharam Dutt's hold over the village, his repeated orders to have Gautam killed, and the bribery rumour spread by his brother Bagga that turns the villagers against Gautam while he is away.
lover_boy_explanation: The film is about a police officer reforming a village and discovering a brother, and the romance develops alongside that rather than driving it. Gautam's defining acts are official and fraternal; the attachment is a reward rather than a motivation.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The relationship is given a slow build that the genre rarely allows, and Sandhya's intervention at the climax gives the pairing a payoff most of the batch's secondary romances lack.
actor_transformation: Gautam reveals his true identity to Sandhya before confronting Govinda, which is the one moment he trusts anyone with it.
female_transformation: Sandhya moves from respect to love, and is the person who reveals Gautam's identity to Govinda and Ganga, which turns the climax.
relationship_outcome: Intact; she is instrumental in the rescue that resolves the film.
relationship_analysis: A secondary romance that nonetheless does narrative work: Sandhya is the only person Gautam tells who he is, and her disclosure to Govinda and Ganga is what converts the enforcer into a rescuer. That is a materially higher function than most heroines in this batch are given, and the female-agency score reflects it.
critical_reading: The film follows the convention in which a village woman's love is earned by a man's public virtue rather than by anything between them, but it departs from convention by making her the holder of the secret that resolves the plot rather than the hostage who occasions it.

initial_relationship: A Pathan chieftain and the Anglo-Indian girl he takes into his house by force
how_they_meet: Javed seizes Ruth and her family from the Hindu household sheltering them after the massacre of the British at church, and brings them to his own house.
courtship_pattern: Not courtship: possession first, and then a slow, watched, half-permitted attachment inside a household where she is effectively captive.
emotional_dynamic: Obsession on his side, which the title names, and something unresolved on hers, conducted under the eyes of his wife and her mother.
pair_conflict: She is a captive, he is married, and her mother has made the marriage conditional on an Indian victory.
pair_friction_explanation: The relationship is founded on force and conducted under duress, which is friction of a structural kind even where the film shows tenderness. The plot records a simmering affair rather than open conflict between them, but the imbalance of power is total.
external_opposition_source: War or politics; Family; Religion; Community
external_opposition_explanation: The 1857 rebellion itself, on whose outcome Miriam makes the marriage conditional; Javed's wife Firdaus; his politically committed brother-in-law Sarfaraz, who destroys his pigeon coops when the Indian forces lose; and the religious and communal gulf between a Pathan household and an Anglo-Indian family in hiding.
lover_boy_explanation: The obsession is total and the character is organised entirely around it, which is the archetype's intensity, but it is expressed through abduction and possession rather than courtship or devotion. Scored above the midpoint for the completeness of the fixation and held down by what the fixation actually consists of.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; the retrospective notice located calls the film a bittersweet, entirely futile love story without assessing the performers. The pairing works because Kapoor plays the obsession as helplessness rather than swagger, which keeps a coercive situation legible as tragedy.
actor_transformation: From a chieftain indifferent to the rebellion to a man who needs it to succeed for private reasons, and who is destroyed with it.
female_transformation: Ruth passes from a fugitive to a captive to the object of a bargain struck over her by her mother and her captor.
relationship_outcome: Futile. The British win, the condition fails, and the attachment ends with the rebellion.
relationship_analysis: The most artistically regarded film in the batch and the most ethically complicated pairing in the filmography so far. Junoon means obsession, and the film is candid that what Javed feels is not courtship: he takes Ruth by force and then waits on a war to legitimise it. That Kapoor produced it, and cast his own wife as the mother who negotiates the bargain, makes it the clearest statement of his ambitions as a producer of serious cinema.
critical_reading: The film is markedly more clear-eyed than its contemporaries about the coercion at the centre of its romance, declining to convert the abduction into consent or to reward the obsession. A modern reading can still note that Ruth remains largely an object of the men's and her mother's negotiations, and that the film's sympathy for Javed's futility is more developed than its interest in what the arrangement costs her.

initial_relationship: Married, with her brother living in the household
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage predates the film.
courtship_pattern: None. The marriage is established and the film shows it only under the pressure of Javed's obsession.
emotional_dynamic: A wife watching her husband install another woman in their house and fall in love with her, with the household's customs preventing her from refusing the guests.
pair_conflict: Javed's pursuit of Ruth, conducted inside the marital home.
pair_friction_explanation: Severe and sustained, though largely silent: the plot records Firdaus's jealousy and her watchful suspicion as a continuous presence through the second half. The injury is unambiguous and it is entirely her husband's doing.
external_opposition_explanation: The rebellion that brought the Labadoors into the house, and the Pathan obligation of hospitality and sanctuary that her brother invokes to keep them there over his own objections.
lover_boy_explanation: Toward Firdaus the character shows no romantic conduct whatever: the marriage is the thing his obsession is conducted across. Scored near the floor because the relationship exists and is not hostile, only abandoned.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Shabana Azmi is given little dialogue in the relationship and plays it almost entirely in observation, which makes the marriage register as a standing rebuke to the romance the film is ostensibly about.
actor_transformation: None toward Firdaus; the film's changes in Javed are all directed elsewhere.
female_transformation: Firdaus moves from wife to witness, holding the household together around a husband who has stopped attending to it.
relationship_outcome: The marriage survives the obsession because the obsession fails, not because anything between them is repaired.
relationship_analysis: A second row for Junoon is warranted because Firdaus is not a briefly glimpsed spouse: her jealousy is named in the plot as one of the forces the household runs on, and her presence is what makes the central romance a transgression rather than a courtship. The pairing carries the batch's sharpest contrast, a marriage with high friction and no romance beside an obsession with high centrality and no consent.
critical_reading: The film is more interested in Javed's futility than in Firdaus's position, and gives her endurance rather than recourse. Read now, she is the person with the strongest claim in the story and the least voice in it, and the Pathan hospitality code that the film treats as noble is precisely what obliges her to house her husband's obsession.

initial_relationship: A mine engineer and a press reporter covering the mine
how_they_meet: Not dramatised in detail; Anita is a press reporter and photographer working around the colliery where Ravi is the engineer.
courtship_pattern: A light thread running beside the main action, one of three romances the film distributes among its three male leads.
emotional_dynamic: Companionable and untroubled; the film gives the relationship no crisis of its own.
pair_conflict: None recorded.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair appears in the article's plot account. The film's antagonisms are between the miners and the owner, and among the three men.
external_opposition_explanation: No family, class or personal obstacle is placed against the pair. What threatens them is the mine itself, which threatens everyone in the film equally.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi's function is professional and civic: he runs the pit, takes the workers' side against the owner and leads the rescue. The romance is a genre requirement rather than a motivation, and nothing he does in the film is done for Anita.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Anita is written as a working journalist rather than an ornament, which gives the scenes a brisk equality, but the film's attention is on the disaster and on Bachchan's Vijay.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: Intact; Ravi survives the flooding with an injured leg.
relationship_analysis: The third romance in a film that gives one to each of its three male leads, and the clearest illustration of the late-1970s pattern in Kapoor's work: romance centrality of three, friction of one, opposition of three, and a character whose real relationships are with the men he works beside. Anita's profession as a reporter gives her more independent standing than the score for centrality suggests.
critical_reading: Distributing a romance to each hero is the multi-starrer's way of servicing its stars rather than its story, and all three women here, a doctor, a reporter and a bangle seller, are given occupations and then very little to do with them. The film's genuine subject, industrial negligence at Chasnala, has no room for any of them.

actress_prominence: Female lead, in a double role
initial_relationship: Strangers; he stops to repair her broken-down car
how_they_meet: Rekha's car breaks down while she is driving through her own estate and Prem, who has a gift for machines, fixes it.
who_initiates: Mutual, over a series of meetings
courtship_pattern: A few chance meetings on the estate, then love, then an engagement announced abruptly enough to surprise the whole household.
emotional_dynamic: Ardent on both sides and, from the household's point of view, suspiciously rapid.
pair_conflict: Nothing between them while she is alive; afterwards, the suspicion that he arranged her death.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple themselves never quarrel. The friction is the audience's and the investigators': Prem is absent at the engagement when the police inspector arrives, and absent from the houseboat when she is pushed into the lake, which makes him a suspect rather than an antagonist.
external_opposition_explanation: An unidentified murderer inside the household, the estate's servants and managers, and Kishore's determination to marry Rashmi, whose inheritance depends on Rekha's arrangements. The attempt on Rekha's life is the opposition made literal.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is a romantic lead in a thriller, and its most telling moment is Prem declaring his intense love for the dead Rekha to a woman he believes is her sister. Devotion is present but is deployed as evidence in a mystery rather than as the character's purpose.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film asks Kapoor to be simultaneously ardent and plausibly guilty, and the courtship is played warmly enough that the suspicion has something to work against; Rekha carries the more demanding assignment, playing her own sister investigating her own murder.
actor_transformation: From suitor to suspect, and his constancy to the dead Rekha is what finally tells against the suspicion.
female_transformation: Rekha survives the attempt, takes her sister's identity, and investigates her own murder, including by testing the man she was to marry.
relationship_outcome: Prem is cleared when the murderer is revealed in the climax.
relationship_analysis: A romance built to be doubted, and a rare instance in this filmography of the woman holding the investigative position: Rekha interrogates her own fiance while disguised as her sister. Female agency is scored high for that, and pair friction stays low because the couple never actually oppose each other.
critical_reading: The film's pleasure is in a woman auditing the man who says he loves her, which is a sharper premise than the genre usually allows; it retreats from it by making him innocent and the murderer someone else, so the test she conducts changes nothing she believed.

initial_relationship: A school's dance teacher and the new music teacher, who is a burglar in disguise
how_they_meet: Sunil joins the school as Lakshman, the music teacher, on a job to abduct a pupil, and meets Shalu, who teaches dance there.
courtship_pattern: A staffroom courtship conducted entirely under a false name and a false purpose.
emotional_dynamic: Light and comic, with the deception known only to him until she discovers it.
pair_conflict: He is at the school to kidnap a child, and she finds out.
pair_friction_explanation: No hostility, but a real breach: she learns his identity and motive, and the film's turn is that she and Anju talk the two men out of the crime rather than denouncing them. The friction is the discovery and its aftermath, compressed and comic.
external_opposition_explanation: Uncle Jagdish, Sunil's boss, who loses patience and abducts the boy himself, and the rival gang employing Vijay. The criminal world both men belong to is what stands between the courtship and any future.
lover_boy_explanation: The courtship is substantial and the reform it produces is the film's moral engine, but Sunil is a comic burglar first and the relationship with the child does as much work as the romance. A romantic lead in an action comedy rather than a devotee.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Hema Malini, in their sixth film together, play the impersonation comedy lightly, and the pairing works better as farce than as romance; the film's real double act is Kapoor and Bachchan.
actor_transformation: Shalu's word, with Anju's, is what turns Sunil off the kidnapping; the reform is explicitly credited to the two women.
female_transformation: Shalu moves from a woman courted under a false identity to one who changes the man rather than reporting him.
relationship_outcome: The boy is rescued, the boss arrested, and the couples are left intact.
relationship_analysis: One of the few comedies in this stretch where the heroines are given the film's decisive moral act: the article states plainly that the two women change the men for good by their word. That lifts the female-agency score well above the norm for Kapoor's 1980 output, even though the romance itself is thinly drawn.
critical_reading: The reform-by-good-woman device gives Shalu and Anju agency of a narrow kind, the power to improve men rather than to pursue anything of their own, and the film shows neither woman outside the school or the couple. It is still a marked improvement on the hostage heroines of the surrounding action films.

initial_relationship: One of three childhood friends who all come to love the same woman
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the article records that Vijay, Jeet and Ajay each love Rekha at different moments and that she reciprocates Vijay's feeling.
courtship_pattern: Not shown in detail. The attachment is stated and then overtaken by the criminal plot.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual, and then suspended when she accepts another man out of obligation.
pair_conflict: Rekha accepts Jeet's proposal in gratitude after his father secures her own father's acquittal.
pair_friction_explanation: Not antagonism but a displacement: she is the one who chooses Vijay and then accepts Jeet, for reasons of debt rather than feeling. The article records the sequence without describing a quarrel between them.
external_opposition_explanation: Mohanlal Saxena, Jeet's father, a criminal behind a respectable front, who has Rekha's father framed and then cleared, engineers the marriage proposal that follows, and has Vijay's brother killed.
lover_boy_explanation: The attachment is real and is the reason the three friendships fracture, but the second half is a revenge plot over a murdered brother. Romance is the cause of the rift rather than the character's continuing motivation.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The article's plot gives the relationship a sentence and then moves to the men's rivalry; there is little in the documented material on which to base more than a neutral reading, and the film was a failure that attracted no writing.
actor_transformation: Not attributable to the relationship; Vijay's change is driven by his brother's murder.
female_transformation: Rekha moves from choosing Vijay to accepting Jeet out of gratitude for her father's acquittal.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the film closes on Jeet's death shielding Vijay rather than on the romance.
relationship_analysis: A triangle in which the woman's choice is overridden by a debt her family owes, and in which the film's interest is entirely in what happens between the three men afterwards. The pattern, a woman transferred between men as settlement of an obligation, recurs across this filmography from Patanga onward.
critical_reading: Rekha's acceptance of Jeet is presented as gratitude and therefore as creditable, which is how the period's scripts convert a woman's coerced choice into a virtue. The film never returns to ask what she wanted, and its resolution is a death between two men.

initial_relationship: A con man and a woman running a con of her own
how_they_meet: Ravi and Vijay meet her at a restaurant, where she is being pressed for a debt of Rs 30,000 by a middle-aged man; Ravi is attracted to her.
courtship_pattern: Not courtship so much as mutual professional recognition: he tries to rescue her, discovers she has swindled him, and the two parties merge their operations.
emotional_dynamic: Light, wary and transactional, warming once the pretences are dropped on both sides.
pair_conflict: She and her uncle take the brothers for Rs 5,000 with a stolen car and a fake debt.
pair_friction_explanation: The deception is mutual and is treated as a professional courtesy rather than a betrayal: the brothers are impressed enough to propose a partnership. Nothing that follows is played as a grievance between them.
external_opposition_explanation: Shakaal, whose killing of the brothers' eldest sibling turns the whole group from confidence tricksters into avengers, and the island operation they eventually have to breach.
lover_boy_explanation: The film is a heist-and-revenge picture built on three men, and the attraction is a few scenes in the first act. Nothing in Ravi's arc is driven by Renu, and the relationship all but disappears once the revenge plot begins.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The scenes are brisk and the joke, that each is trying to swindle the other, gives the pairing more to play than most third-act-free romances in this filmography; the film's attention is elsewhere from the midpoint on.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the relationship.
female_transformation: Renu moves from running a con on the brothers to joining their operation.
relationship_outcome: Not separately resolved; she is part of the group by the end.
relationship_analysis: Notable mainly because the woman is a confidence trickster rather than a victim: Renu's debt, her name and her car are all fabrications, and she takes the brothers' money before they take hers. The female-agency score is unusually high for a romance this peripheral.
critical_reading: Having established a heroine who is nobody's dupe, the film promptly absorbs her into a male gang and gives her nothing to do in the assault that forms its climax. That pattern, a capable woman introduced and then parked, recurs across the multi-starrers of this period.

initial_relationship: His first wife, comatose in an institution for fourteen years
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage predates the film and is interrupted by her fall.
courtship_pattern: None. The relationship exists as an unresolved first marriage running underneath a second one.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine affection on his side, expressed almost entirely as the wish not to harm her with the truth.
pair_conflict: He has married her sister in her absence, and the household is staged to conceal it from her.
pair_friction_explanation: Severe once she recovers, though it is never a quarrel: the injury is the concealment itself, and when it comes out she loses consciousness, becomes violent, and has to be sent back to the institution. The damage is total and it was done, however defensibly, by him.
external_opposition_explanation: The fall that put her in a coma for fourteen years, the doctor's decision not to tell her of the second marriage, and the presence of her sister as the current wife. The obstacle is circumstance compounded by a family conspiracy of silence.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no courtship and no romantic conduct toward Sharada; Balraj's behaviour is entirely protective and evasive. The role is a husband managing an impossible domestic arrangement, not a lover.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, though Raakhee was nominated for the Filmfare Best Actress award for the film. The relationship is played almost entirely in what is withheld, and Raakhee's final turn, feigning madness to release the household, is the performance the nomination recognised.
actor_transformation: From a man relieved at his wife's recovery to one who must return her to an institution to keep his household standing.
female_transformation: Sharada wakes into a world fourteen years on, discovers her sister has her husband, and finally acts by pretending to be mad so that she can leave them to it.
relationship_outcome: She is returned to the institution and, as Sarita discovers, is play-acting her madness in order to exit the family.
relationship_analysis: The first of two rows for this film. The pairing is among the most quietly devastating in the filmography: a marriage that never ended, a wife who was never told, and a resolution in which she feigns insanity to release her husband and her sister. Her deception, unlike his, is an act of will, which is why female agency scores high against a very low health score.
critical_reading: The film's sympathy is arranged around Balraj's impossible position and Purnima's sacrifice in dressing as a widow, while the person actually deprived of fourteen years and then of her husband is asked to withdraw quietly. That the script gives Sharada the dignity of choosing her own exit is its best decision, and it is made almost in passing.

initial_relationship: His second wife, and his first wife's younger sister
how_they_meet: Purnima is Sharada's younger sister, widowed young; she and Balraj married after years in which Sharada showed no sign of recovering.
who_initiates: Not recorded; the marriage follows the loss of hope for Sharada
courtship_pattern: None shown. The marriage is settled and happy when the film opens.
emotional_dynamic: A contented middle-aged marriage that is asked, without warning, to pretend it does not exist.
pair_conflict: Nothing between them; the strain is that Sharada's recovery requires Purnima to unmake her own position in the house.
pair_friction_explanation: The couple are entirely aligned and act together throughout, including in the deception. Balraj's distress at seeing her in a widow's clothes is the closest the film comes to friction between them, and it is sympathy rather than conflict.
external_opposition_explanation: Sharada's recovery, which makes the marriage unspeakable; the doctor's instruction to conceal it; and the elaborate reconstruction of the household as it stood fourteen years earlier, with Purnima dressed as a widow and her own son sent away to Sarita's hostel.
lover_boy_explanation: A settled husband in a domestic drama, with no courtship, pursuit or romantic display. What the role expresses is partnership under pressure, which is the opposite pole of the archetype from Jab Jab Phool Khile.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Rekha play a marriage of long standing rather than an attraction, and the film asks them to convey it while acting out its absence; the scenes of Purnima in widow's dress with Balraj unable to look at her are where the pairing registers.
actor_transformation: Balraj holds the arrangement together and is finally forced to abandon it when the truth escapes.
female_transformation: Purnima erases herself, resuming a widow's clothes and sending away her own child, to protect the sister whose husband she married.
relationship_outcome: The marriage survives; Sharada is returned to the institution.
relationship_analysis: The second row for Baseraa, and the reason the film needs two: Kapoor's character is married to both sisters within the same house, one legally and one in memory, and the drama is entirely in how the two marriages cannot occupy the same room. The pairing with Purnima scores high on mutuality and health precisely because its cost is paid by the other woman.
critical_reading: Purnima's sacrifice is the film's emotional centrepiece and is also, on inspection, the erasure of a woman's marriage and motherhood to spare her sister's feelings, undertaken on a doctor's advice and a husband's consent. The film admires it without asking whether anyone might simply have told Sharada the truth.

initial_relationship: A CBI officer and a woman who had been an associate of the don he is hunting
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the article records only that one of Vicky's associates, Neera, marries the CBI officer Kumar Sahni, and that this changes the direction of the story.
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The marriage is reported rather than dramatised.
emotional_dynamic: Not developed by the article's summary; the marriage functions as a structural connection between the police and the underworld.
pair_conflict: Her past with Vicky, and her discovery years later that he is alive and living as a healer near her in-laws.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is recorded, but the marriage carries an unresolved connection to the man her husband was hunting, and it is she, not he, who finds Vicky alive. The friction is latent rather than enacted.
external_opposition_explanation: Vicky himself, whose survival puts Neera in the position of being the only witness, and the criminal organisation she was once part of.
lover_boy_explanation: The film belongs to Dharmendra's Vicky, whose own lost love drives it. Kapoor's officer is a husband and an investigator with no courtship and no romantic arc of his own.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The article's summary reports the marriage in a single clause and gives the couple no scenes to characterise, so there is little documented basis for more than a neutral assessment.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Neera moves from a don's associate to a CBI officer's wife, and then to the person who recognises him in his new life.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the summary ends on Vicky's decision about the only witness to his survival.
relationship_analysis: A marriage that exists to connect two halves of a plot: the woman who knew the don becomes the wife of the officer chasing him, and is then the one who finds him. It is a thin pairing, entered because the article gives the marriage explicit structural weight, and most categorical fields are marked unclear.
critical_reading: Neera is positioned between two men as the hinge of the plot, and the summary's framing, that the don must decide whether to kill this only witness, reduces her to a liability to be managed. The film's emotional investment is in Vicky's murdered first love rather than in the living wife.

initial_relationship: Engaged to be married
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Shekhar introduces his fiancee Shobha to his brother Amit, and the three form a close friendship.
courtship_pattern: Settled before the film opens; what is shown is the camaraderie between the engaged couple and Shekhar's brother.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and uncomplicated, and the only unshadowed relationship in the film.
pair_conflict: None. The relationship is ended by his death, not by anything between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict of any kind is recorded. The engagement is happy and brief, and the film's every subsequent complication flows from its interruption rather than from any flaw in it.
external_opposition_explanation: The Indo-Pakistani War of 1971, in which Shekhar is killed before the marriage, leaving Shobha pregnant and unmarried and creating the social exposure that Amit marries her to prevent.
lover_boy_explanation: Shekhar is an uncomplicatedly loving fiance and nothing else: there is no pursuit, obstacle or sacrifice, and the part is short. Scored at the midpoint as a straightforwardly romantic role with very little screen time in which to be one.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film needs the engagement to register quickly and warmly so that its loss can drive everything after, and Kapoor and Jaya Bachchan supply that economically; they have few scenes before he is killed.
actor_transformation: None; he dies in the first movement.
female_transformation: Shobha passes from a happily engaged woman to a pregnant widow-in-effect, married to her fiance's brother to spare her the stigma, and then into a passionless marriage she comes to value.
relationship_outcome: Ended by Shekhar's death in the 1971 war.
relationship_analysis: The shortest consequential pairing in the filmography: Kapoor's character is dead within the first movement, and the entire film, an adultery drama about his brother, exists because of it. It is the clearest case for scoring narrative weight separately from screen time, since the romance is minor in duration and foundational in effect.
critical_reading: Shobha's pregnancy is treated by the film as a problem of social exposure to be solved by a substitute husband, and the arrangement is made between brothers and circumstance rather than by her. The film is more interested in Amit's divided heart than in the woman married twice over to manage a scandal.

initial_relationship: Married, with a history on her side he does not know about
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Kalpana marries the industrialist Kumar after her relationship with Raman, her pregnancy and her attempted suicide.
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The film's interest begins with the marriage and the blackmail that follows it.
emotional_dynamic: A wealthy, apparently settled marriage carrying a secret and a blackmailer.
pair_conflict: Shivnath's blackmail over photographs of Kalpana with Raman, and the history she has not told her husband.
pair_friction_explanation: The strain is substantial and sits between them, since it consists of what she is concealing, but it is resolved by her own disclosure rather than by a confrontation. The film ends with Shivnath guilty and the marriage intact.
external_opposition_explanation: Shivnath, a struggling photographer married to Kalpana's former roommate, who holds photographs of her with Raman and blackmails her with them, and Raman himself, who reappears as a taxi driver and helps her after an accident.
