lover_boy_explanation: Kumar is a husband rather than a suitor: no courtship is shown, and his function is to be the man to whom the truth is eventually told. The romantic content is in Kalpana's past, not in his conduct.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film is Reena Roy's, with Kapoor as the stable point she finally confides in; the pairing is written as security rather than attraction and is played accordingly.
actor_transformation: From an unknowing husband to one told everything and remaining.
female_transformation: Kalpana moves from concealment and vulnerability to blackmail, to telling her husband the whole of it herself.
relationship_outcome: She reveals everything to Kumar and Shivnath is left guilty; the marriage holds.
relationship_analysis: One of a small group of films in which Kapoor plays the husband who is told a difficult truth and does not punish the teller. Set against Satyam Shivam Sundaram, made four years earlier, the contrast is instructive: the same actor, a comparable revelation, and the opposite response.
critical_reading: The film treats a woman's pre-marital relationship and pregnancy as a secret requiring blackmail and confession, which is the period's standard moral arithmetic. What distinguishes it is that the disclosure is hers to make and that the husband's acceptance, rather than her punishment, is the resolution.

initial_relationship: A long marriage across a cultural divide, already failing
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage of a Punjabi Sikh man and a Maharashtrian Hindu woman predates the film.
courtship_pattern: None. The film opens on a marriage in difficulty and observes it through their adolescent son.
emotional_dynamic: Estrangement conducted in front of a teenager who reads it as the condition of his own life.
pair_conflict: A marriage neither can repair, and a son caught between them.
pair_friction_explanation: Sustained marital conflict is the film's domestic premise, and it is severe enough that escaping it is part of why Angad leaves for the Air Force. The article describes marital problems rather than a rupture, so the score stops short of the highest band.
external_opposition_explanation: The cultural distance the film foregrounds, a clean-shaven Sikh married to a Hindu with a Sikh son, is context rather than active opposition; no third party works against the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Nihal is a father and a difficult husband, with no courtship, devotion or romantic display of any kind. The role is deliberately unromantic, and Kapoor cast himself in it as the film's producer.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the notices located address the film's treatment of the Air Force rather than its performances. Kapoor and Rekha, in their fifth film together, play a failing marriage with a flatness that suits Nihalani's register.
actor_transformation: Nihal is reconciled to his son's choice, which is the film's concession to him; the marriage itself is not repaired on screen.
female_transformation: Neelima's position is observed rather than resolved.
relationship_outcome: Unresolved as a marriage; the film's closure belongs to Angad.
relationship_analysis: The lowest lover-boy score Kapoor had taken in a leading role to this point, in a film he produced and in which he cast his own son as the protagonist. It belongs with The Householder, Abhinetri and Baseraa in the group where he plays a husband, and it is the least flattering of them.
critical_reading: The film uses the parents' marriage as the condition its protagonist must grow out of, which gives Neelima little existence beyond her difficulty; the coming-of-age structure requires the adults to be static. That Kapoor, as producer, took the unsympathetic parental role rather than the heroic one is the more interesting decision.

initial_relationship: Married
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage predates the film.
courtship_pattern: None. The marriage exists to supply the motive the prosecution attributes to him.
emotional_dynamic: Not developed; the couple's function is to be the reason a murder charge looks plausible.
pair_conflict: None between them; the pressure comes from Prem Oberoi's pursuit of Kalpana and the charge that follows his death.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between husband and wife is recorded. The film's antagonism is between Shekhar and a dead man's reputation, and between the lawyer and the real killer.
external_opposition_explanation: Prem Oberoi, who was lustful toward Kalpana, and the murder charge his death produces, which carries a plausible motive for a husband. The real culprit, the steward Suresh Talwar, killed Prem over his own fiancee and then killed her as a witness.
lover_boy_explanation: A courtroom drama in which Kapoor's character is largely passive and the active role belongs to Raj Kapoor's advocate. The marriage is a plot premise, not a romance the film examines.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film gives the marriage almost no screen time of its own, existing as it does to establish a motive; the picture's interest is in the courtroom and in the rare pairing of Shashi Kapoor with his eldest brother.
actor_transformation: None.
female_transformation: None recorded.
relationship_outcome: The marriage survives; Shekhar is acquitted of all charges.
relationship_analysis: A marriage that exists as a motive. The pairing is recorded because the wife's harassment by the victim is the reason the charge sticks, but the film has no interest in the relationship itself, and its distinction is that it puts Shashi and Raj Kapoor on screen together as actors.
critical_reading: Kalpana is pursued by one man, avenged by a plot she has no part in, and cleared of nothing because she was never accused; the script treats a woman's harassment purely as a fact about her husband's legal exposure.

initial_relationship: A hotel owner and the dancer hired to kill him
how_they_meet: Raja meets Nisha, a young dancer, at his hotel and is attracted to her; she has been engaged by Ranjit Singh to murder him.
who_initiates: Raja, unknowingly, and Nisha under instruction
courtship_pattern: An approach engineered as an assassination, which the assassin abandons because she falls in love with the target.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine attraction on his side and a job on hers, until the job becomes impossible.
pair_conflict: She is under contract to kill him, and arranges a party on a boat to do it.
pair_friction_explanation: The deception is lethal and one-sided, and it persists to the point of a staged opportunity to murder him. It is scored in the middle band because Nisha never acts on it and the film treats her change of heart as the resolution rather than as a betrayal to be answered.
external_opposition_explanation: Ranjit Singh, son of the man who murdered Raja's father, who hired Nisha and later kidnaps the family to force a transfer of property, and the long conspiracy over the estate that has surrounded Raja since infancy.
lover_boy_explanation: Kapoor is second lead in a Bachchan masala vehicle, and the romance is one strand of a plot about a stolen inheritance and a mother's sacrifice. Raja is charming and genuinely attached, but the film's emotional weight is on Savitri and Arjun.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Parveen Babi had by this point made several films together and the rapport is easy, though the script keeps Nisha's real purpose hidden and gives the pairing little room to be anything but pleasant until the reversal.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the romance; Raja's change comes from learning the truth about Savitri.
female_transformation: Nisha moves from a hired killer to a woman who cannot carry out the contract and is finally married to her target.
relationship_outcome: Raja marries Nisha at the end, alongside Arjun's marriage to Poonam.
relationship_analysis: The assassin-who-falls-in-love device, and a late instance of the pattern in which Kapoor's character is loved by a woman concealing her purpose, as in Fakira. The film forgives the deception entirely and marries them, which is the masala convention working at full strength.
critical_reading: Nisha is introduced as an instrument of the villain and redeemed by falling for the hero, so her entire characterisation is a function of what men want from her. That the film never requires her to answer for the contract is typical of how the period's masala scripts dispose of a heroine's culpability.

initial_relationship: A police officer and the daughter of the country's most powerful smuggler
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the article records that Sonia falls in love with Ravi Malhotra, a police officer, and wants to marry him.
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The attachment is stated and functions as one of the two choices by which Dhanpat Rai's children reject his world.
emotional_dynamic: Not developed by the article's summary.
pair_conflict: None between them; the obstacle is entirely her father.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is recorded. The film's question is the father's, whether children's happiness matters more than power and money, and the couple are aligned on one side of it.
external_opposition_explanation: Dhanpat Rai Mehta, described as the country's most powerful smuggler, surrounded by a fortress of power and money, whose daughter proposes to marry the police officer whose job is to destroy him.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is the character's whole function in the film, which gives it weight, but Kapoor is third-billed and the part is written as a position in the father's dilemma rather than as a performance of devotion.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The article's plot summary is four sentences and gives the couple no scenes to characterise, so the score reflects the absence of documented material rather than a judgement about the playing.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Sonia chooses a police officer over her father's world, which is one half of the film's central question.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the summary says only that Dhanpat Rai's question is answered soon.
relationship_analysis: A structurally pure version of the pattern that has organised Kapoor's romances since Jab Jab Phool Khile: zero friction inside the couple, very high opposition from the woman's father, and a resolution that depends on the father changing rather than on the couple doing anything. Here it is doubled, since his son's engagement to a poor girl poses the same question.
critical_reading: The film frames the daughter's choice as a test of her father's values rather than as her own act, and the title question, what matters more, is addressed entirely to him. Sonia's love is the occasion for a man's moral crisis.

initial_relationship: Married with two children; she is a judge
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage is settled when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None. The film opens on a quiet small-town household and breaks it.
emotional_dynamic: A settled marriage confronted with a seven-year-old child from an affair its wife knew nothing about.
pair_conflict: Prem brings home a son by another woman, and a blackmailer threatens to tell Bhavna and the children how he came by him.
pair_friction_explanation: Severe and direct: the film's second half is Prem confronted by his wife on one side and his children on the other over a child produced by an affair he concealed for seven years. The injury is unambiguous and it is his.
external_opposition_explanation: Prakash Dutt, the blackmailer demanding a large sum to keep the affair quiet, and Sneh's terminal cancer, which is what forces the child into the household in the first place.
lover_boy_explanation: There is no courtship anywhere in the film and Prem's conduct toward his wife consists of concealment followed by an unavoidable disclosure. The role is a husband in the wrong, with the romantic content displaced into a past affair.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Casting Raakhee as a judge gives the wife an authority the confrontation needs, and the pairing plays best in the scenes where her professional composure is what Prem has to face.
actor_transformation: From a man with a concealed past to one whose household contains the evidence of it.
female_transformation: Bhavna moves from an unknowing wife to the person who must decide what the marriage and the household will do with the boy.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the article's plot ends inside the confrontation.
relationship_analysis: The first of two rows for this film, which needs both because its subject is the collision between a marriage and a seven-year relationship that produced a child. The wife being a judge is the script's sharpest idea, putting the person best equipped to weigh the case in the position of being unable to be impartial about it.
critical_reading: The film's sympathies are arranged around Prem's decency in taking the boy in, which quietly converts a seven-year deception into an act of responsibility. The two women are set against each other, one dying and one wronged, and the narrative's attention stays on the man deciding between them.

initial_relationship: A seven-year relationship outside his marriage, conducted in another city
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the article records that Sneh has known Prem for seven years and lives in Bombay, and that their son is now seven years old.
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The relationship is established entirely in retrospect, by a letter delivered after seven years.
emotional_dynamic: Sustained attachment conducted at a distance and in secret, surfacing only when she is dying.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them; what ends it is her illness.
pair_friction_explanation: The article records no conflict between Prem and Sneh. Their relationship is presented as long-standing and settled in its own terms, and it is terminal illness rather than discord that brings it into the open.
external_opposition_explanation: Prem's marriage to Bhavna and his two children by her, Sneh's cancer and the expectation that she will not live long, and Prakash Dutt's blackmail once the connection becomes usable.
lover_boy_explanation: A sustained clandestine attachment and the acceptance of a child are real commitments, which lifts the score above the marital rows, but everything about the relationship is retrospective and none of it is shown as courtship or devotion on screen.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The relationship is conveyed through a letter, a meeting and a handover rather than through courtship scenes, so what Kapoor and Zeenat Aman have to play is the residue of an attachment rather than the attachment itself.
actor_transformation: Prem accepts the son and takes him into his marital home, which is the act the rest of the film is about.
female_transformation: Sneh moves from a woman who has kept both the child and the connection to herself for seven years to one who discloses both in order to secure the boy's future, and leaves for treatment in America.
relationship_outcome: Ends with her illness and departure; the child passes to Prem.
relationship_analysis: The second row for Bandhan Kuchchey Dhaagon Ka, whose title, the bond of loose threads, describes exactly this arrangement. Together with the marital row it gives the clearest instance in the filmography of a Kapoor character sustaining two relationships in parallel, with the film's mechanism being the moment they are forced into the same house.
critical_reading: Sneh is given a terminal illness at precisely the moment her existence becomes inconvenient, which is the period's standard method of resolving a mistress: she discloses, hands over the child and leaves the country. Her seven years and her motherhood are treated as a problem the wife must absorb.

initial_relationship: A ruling prince and the wife of a British colonial official in his district
how_they_meet: The Nawab invites the Anglo-Indian officials and their wives to a dinner party at his palace, where Olivia attracts his attention.
courtship_pattern: A courtship conducted across the colonial divide, through palace invitations and the mediation of his English friend Harry, against the disapproval of the entire British station.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual and illicit, sustained by her boredom with memsahib society and her fascination with India, and by his charm and idleness.
pair_conflict: She is married to a British civil servant and he is suspected by that administration of financing bandits.
pair_friction_explanation: The article's lead records an illicit affair rather than a conflict between the pair. What presses on them is external and political; no antagonism between the two is documented.
external_opposition_source: Class; Community; Existing relationship; Crime; War or politics
external_opposition_explanation: The entire apparatus of the Raj: Olivia's marriage to an assistant collector, the memsahib society that bores and watches her, Mrs. Saunders's warning that all Indian men are potential rapists, the racist Dr. Saunders, and the British suspicion that the Nawab shelters the bandits ransacking the region in exchange for a share of their takings.
lover_boy_explanation: The Nawab is a romantic and decadent figure whose pursuit of Olivia is the film's centre, and the affair carries real risk for both. It is held below the higher band because the article documents charm and appetite rather than devotion or sacrifice, and because his political position is a rival preoccupation.
chemistry_explanation: Vincent Canby, reviewing for the New York Times, found the film's modern strand less involving than the story of Olivia and the Nawab, which is an assessment of this pairing's effect relative to the other. The role is also the most conventionally romantic of Kapoor's late English-language parts.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the article carries no plot section and its lead stops at the fact of the affair.
female_transformation: Olivia moves from a young colonial wife bored by the station to a woman conducting an affair that the whole British community would regard as unforgivable.
relationship_outcome: Not stated by the sources consulted. The article has no plot section and its lead establishes the affair without describing how it ends.
relationship_analysis: The last major romantic lead of Kapoor's career and the one that most directly addresses what his English-language films had been circling since Shakespeare Wallah: an Indian man and an Englishwoman, with the colonial relation itself as the obstacle. The film pairs it with a 1982 strand in which Olivia's great-niece has an affair with a married Indian man, so the transgression is deliberately doubled across sixty years.
critical_reading: The film is knowing about the erotic charge the Raj invested in exactly this transgression, and it places Mrs. Saunders's warning that all Indian men are potential rapists in the mouth of a character it has already marked as morbid. What it cannot fully escape is that the Nawab remains a figure of decadent fascination, written partly from Forster's and Ackerley's accounts of their own Indian princes.

initial_relationship: Married; he is settled in Toronto and she is newly arrived from India
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Arun, an Indian in Toronto, marries a traditional Indian woman.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The film begins with the marriage and proceeds to its failure.
emotional_dynamic: A marriage that cannot survive the wife's inability to settle in a country the husband has already made his own.
pair_conflict: Shobha cannot fit into Canadian life and comes to suspect Arun of an affair with his secretary.
pair_friction_explanation: Substantial and terminal for twenty years: the suspicion is hers, the failure to adapt is hers, and the separation divides the children between two countries. The article does not describe quarrels, but the outcome is a marriage abandoned.
external_opposition_explanation: Emigration itself, which the film treats as the corrosive agent, the cultural distance between Toronto and the life Shobha knows, and twenty years later the gang whose kidnapping of their daughter forces the family back together.
lover_boy_explanation: No courtship, pursuit or devotion is shown; Arun is a husband who loses a marriage to geography and suspicion and spends the rest of the film as a father. The romantic register is absent by design.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Sharmila Tagore, in their seventh and final film together, are asked to play estrangement rather than attraction, and the accumulated familiarity of six earlier pairings does most of the work of suggesting a shared past.
actor_transformation: From a husband whose wife leaves him to a father reunited with the whole family through a crisis.
female_transformation: Shobha leaves Canada with her son, raises him without telling him who his father is, and returns twenty years later into the search for her daughter.
relationship_outcome: Reunited at the end, with Pinky restored to her father, mother and brother.
relationship_analysis: The last of the seven Kapoor and Sharmila Tagore pairings, spanning 1967 to 1983, and the only one about a marriage failing rather than a courtship succeeding. It is also an early Hindi treatment of the emigrant marriage, with the wife's inability to settle presented as the cause.
critical_reading: The film locates the marriage's failure in the woman's refusal or inability to adapt, and in a suspicion it never confirms or denies, so the burden of the separation falls on her while Arun waits twenty years to be vindicated by a reunion. A retrospective Firstpost notice found the film short of the poignancy later diaspora cinema achieved, and the treatment of Shobha is part of why.

initial_relationship: Married, at the head of a joint family
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage is settled when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None. The film opens on a happy joint household and destroys it.
emotional_dynamic: Affectionate and domestic, the emotional centre of a house the family calls a temple of love.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict of any kind is recorded between Prem and Laxmi. The marriage is presented as the household's stable centre, which is what makes his death the catastrophe the rest of the film works against.
external_opposition_explanation: Seth Dharampal, who sets out to cheat the family of its home, and the killing of Prem, which removes the household's head and leaves Laxmi and Ravi to defend it.
lover_boy_explanation: A supporting role as a married elder brother, with no courtship and no romantic display; the part's register is familial. Kapoor is killed partway through and the film belongs to the widow and the surviving brothers.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The marriage has to read as worth defending in a short span before Prem is killed, and Kapoor and Moushumi Chatterjee, in their third film together, establish it efficiently and without ornament.
actor_transformation: None; he is killed.
female_transformation: Laxmi moves from wife to widow and becomes, with Ravi, the defender of the household against Dharampal.
relationship_outcome: Ended by Prem's killing; Laxmi carries the family afterwards.
relationship_analysis: A short, warm marriage whose function is to be destroyed, in the superhit that marked Kapoor's move into supporting roles. The high health and mutuality scores against a low lover-boy score are characteristic of the late filmography: the marriages are good, and he is rarely in them for long.
critical_reading: Widowing the heroine to motivate the surviving brothers is a standard device, and the film does at least give Laxmi the active defence of the house rather than only grief. The contrast with his 1960s leads is stark: by 1984 the romantic function has passed entirely to younger actors in the same films.

initial_relationship: A landowner in Delhi and the man occupying the Kashmir land she has come to repossess
how_they_meet: Aarti travels to Kashmir to take possession of land occupied by Suraj Arora, whose family, her nanny tells her, raised her before her father became wealthy and cut them off.
courtship_pattern: Adversarial arrival, then the discovery of the old family debt, then an attachment formed in the place her father had abandoned.
emotional_dynamic: Antagonism converting quickly to love, complicated by a friend who wants the same man.
pair_conflict: A property claim at the outset, and afterwards Anuradha's competing attachment.
pair_friction_explanation: The initial conflict is a land dispute rather than a personal antagonism, and the article records that all differences are forgotten once she arrives. The continuing friction comes from the triangle rather than from anything between the two of them.
external_opposition_explanation: Aarti's father Karan Singh, who broke with the Arora family once he became wealthy, the property claim that brings her north, and Anuradha, her friend and employee, whose love for Suraj creates a rivalry between the two women.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is the object of two women's attachment in a romance built around him, which is squarely the archetype's position, though the article's account gives him little active courtship and the film's complications belong to the women.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Raakhee's Aarti is written as a Delhi businesswoman with her own establishment, which gives the pairing an adult footing, and Kapoor plays the Kashmir occupier with the unforced ease he had used in the same setting twenty years earlier in Jab Jab Phool Khile.
actor_transformation: Not documented beyond the shift from adversary to lover.
female_transformation: Aarti learns who raised her, abandons the property claim, and then finds herself in competition with her own employee.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the article says the discovery will change everyone's lives and stops there.
relationship_analysis: A late return to the Kashmir romance that made Kapoor a star, with the class positions reversed: here the wealthy party is the woman, the land is hers, and he is the occupier. That inversion, twenty years after Jab Jab Phool Khile, is the most interesting thing about an otherwise conventional triangle.
critical_reading: The film gives Aarti money, a business and a household of her own and then organises the plot around which of two women will get the man, which is how the period's romantic dramas routinely spend a heroine's independence. Anuradha, her employee, is positioned as a rival rather than as a person with a claim of her own.

initial_relationship: Married; he is a police inspector
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage is established when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None. The marriage exists to be destroyed in the opening movement.
emotional_dynamic: Not developed; the article gives the couple no scenes before he is killed.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict is recorded. The marriage is the film's starting condition and is ended by murder within the opening sequence.
external_opposition_explanation: Balvir, the biker-gangster whom Ranjit Singh arrests and who kills him for it and then rapes Sheela. The opposition destroys the marriage outright and sets the entire remaining plot in motion.
lover_boy_explanation: The character is a police officer killed in the opening movement, with no courtship, devotion or romantic action of any kind. Scored near the floor as a husband who exists to be lost.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the article gives the couple almost no screen time together before the killing. The score reflects the near-absence of documented material rather than a judgement about the playing.
actor_transformation: None; he is murdered.
female_transformation: Sheela moves from a police officer's wife to a rape survivor who hires two men to bring her husband's killer to her alive, which is the whole of the film's action.
relationship_outcome: Ended by his murder.
relationship_analysis: Recorded because the marriage and its destruction are the engine of the entire film, not because the relationship is dramatised: Kapoor is third-billed and killed early, and Hema Malini's Sheela carries everything that follows. The external-opposition score of ten reflects opposition that actually causes the death and the assault, which the rubric reserves for exactly this case.
critical_reading: The film uses a woman's rape as the licence for a revenge plot, which was a common and ugly convention of mid-1980s Hindi action cinema. What partially distinguishes it is that the revenge is hers to direct rather than a male relative's, and the men she hires work to her instruction.

initial_relationship: A CBI officer and an advocate who love each other
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the article records that Bhavna loves Ravi Malhotra and that the two become intimate before circumstances separate them.
who_initiates: Not recorded; the article names her love first
courtship_pattern: Not shown. The relationship is established, consummated and broken by circumstance in the space of the summary's opening.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual attachment cut off before it can be acknowledged, leaving her with a child she cannot attribute to him.
pair_conflict: They are separated by circumstances the article does not specify, and she cannot name him as the father.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is recorded and the separation is attributed to circumstance rather than to either party, but the consequences fall entirely on her, and by the film's present action he has married someone else. The friction is in the silence rather than in conflict.
external_opposition_explanation: Ravi's subsequent marriage to Kalpana, Bhavna's inability to name the father of her child, the family name she accepts from Bajrang in order to give her son one, and Bajrang's turn to crime, which makes the man who sheltered her the man Ravi must arrest.
lover_boy_explanation: The romantic content is almost entirely in the past and its consequences fall on the woman; Ravi is a CBI officer married to another woman for the duration of the film. There is no courtship, pursuit or devotion on screen.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the article's summary is written as a series of unanswered questions rather than as a plot. The pairing's affective content is almost wholly retrospective, which leaves little on which to base an assessment.
actor_transformation: Not documented; the summary poses his knowledge of the truth as an open question.
female_transformation: Bhavna moves from an advocate in love to an unmarried mother taking another man's family name to protect her son.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the article's summary ends on a set of questions about what Ravi knows and what becomes of Bhavna.
relationship_analysis: The late-career version of a structure the filmography has used repeatedly since Aa Gale Lag Jaa: an intimacy, a pregnancy, a separation, and a child raised under another arrangement while the father is elsewhere. Here the woman is a practising advocate, which makes her inability to name the father the more pointed.
critical_reading: The consequences of the relationship fall entirely on Bhavna, who bears the child, loses the name and takes a gangster's family name to protect her son, while Ravi marries and continues his career. The summary's closing questions are all about what he knows, which is a fair indication of whose story the film thinks it is telling.

initial_relationship: Married; both are professionals in Delhi
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage is settled when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None. The film is a political thriller and the marriage is its domestic ground.
emotional_dynamic: Two professionals working in parallel, he exposing a political murder and she fighting the case of a woman missing from her in-laws' house.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict is recorded between Vikas and Nisha. The marriage is a working partnership of two people pursuing separate cases, and the film's antagonism is entirely between the press and the political machine.
external_opposition_explanation: Ajay Singh's threats and goons, and the nexus between politicians and media owners that eventually closes on Vikas. The pressure falls on his work rather than on the marriage, though it reaches the household through him.
lover_boy_explanation: The performance that won Kapoor the National Film Award for Best Actor contains almost no romantic content: he is an editor pursuing a story, and the marriage is a settled fact rather than a subject. One of the lowest lover-boy scores in the filmography for a leading role.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Sharmila Tagore, in their eighth and final film together, play a marriage of equals with almost no demonstrativeness, which is precisely what a Gulzar-scripted political thriller requires of it.
actor_transformation: None attributable to the marriage; his change is professional and political.
female_transformation: None recorded; Nisha pursues her own case throughout.
relationship_outcome: Intact; the marriage is not what the film puts at risk.
relationship_analysis: The last significant pairing of Kapoor's career and the one that least resembles the persona he built: a marriage between two working professionals, with a romance-centrality score of three and a female-agency score of eight, in the film that won him the National Award. Set against Jab Jab Phool Khile, twenty-one years earlier, it measures the whole distance the filmography travels.
critical_reading: Nisha is a practising lawyer with a case of her own, and the film neither romanticises nor marginalises her; that the missing woman she is fighting for was declared mad by her in-laws quietly rhymes with the political silencing Vikas is investigating. It is among the few marriages in this filmography written as a partnership rather than as a reward, an obstacle or a loss.

actress_prominence: Principal supporting; the title role belongs to her daughter
initial_relationship: Employer and employee; he is a doctor, she the nurse he hires
how_they_meet: Sharda, having relocated to a small southern town with the daughter she bore alone, finds employment as a nurse with Dr. Rajendra.
courtship_pattern: No courtship at all. The marriage is proposed by Sharda's daughter, who will not marry while her mother has no one, and Rajendra agrees to it.
emotional_dynamic: Respect and practical kindness between two people who have each lost a partner, rather than attraction.
pair_conflict: None recorded between them; the difficulty arriving is Sharda's past, not their marriage.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict of any kind is recorded between Rajendra and Sharda. The marriage is contracted amicably at a third party's request and the household it creates functions; every strain in the film comes from outside it.
external_opposition_explanation: Sharda's history with Satya Prakash, who believed her sold to him and who returns into her life at the end; the concealment of Swati's very existence from Anandi's in-laws; and the community that had already alienated mother and daughter before the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Rajendra is a widower agreeing to a practical marriage arranged by his employee's daughter. There is no courtship, pursuit or romantic declaration anywhere in the part, and his function in the film is to provide a household rather than a romance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor and Sharmila Tagore, in the last of their eight films together, play a marriage of convenience between two middle-aged people with an ease that needs no charge; what registers is familiarity rather than attraction, which is what the part requires.
actor_transformation: From a widowed employer to the head of a blended household containing his own daughter, Sharda and Swati.
female_transformation: Sharda moves from an unmarried mother working as a nurse to a wife in a wealthy household, and then back into the reach of the man she bore a child to.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the summary ends with Satya Prakash's return turning Sharda and Swati's lives upside down.
relationship_analysis: The last Kapoor and Sharmila Tagore pairing, and the inverse of their first: Aamne Samne in 1967 was a courtship conducted under suspicion of murder, and this is a marriage with no courtship at all, proposed by a daughter so that she may marry in turn. It belongs with Alag Alag and Pyar Ki Jeet in the late group where Kapoor is paired on screen with a major actress in a deliberately unromantic relation.
critical_reading: The marriage exists to solve a problem the film has created for its heroine, that a daughter cannot marry while her mother is alone, and both middle-aged parties consent to an arrangement made by a younger woman. It is unusual in treating a second marriage for companionship as unremarkable, and in giving Swati the authority to propose it.

initial_relationship: A happily married couple, he a professor and she a singer
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage is established in flashback as a happy one.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The film opens years after the marriage has already been destroyed and reconstructs it in flashback.
emotional_dynamic: Genuine happiness curdled by a husband's suspicion of his wife's professional partner, and then, years later, by a second suspicion on seeing her in widow's dress.
pair_conflict: Vijay suspects Laxmi's singing partnership with Kumar and forces her out of the house; the misconception is cleared the same day, too late to find her.
pair_friction_explanation: Severe and entirely his doing: he expels his wife from their home over a partnership he has misread, and she is gone before he learns Kumar was marrying someone else. The damage costs them both years and costs him a daughter he does not know about, and when they meet again he misreads her situation a second time.
external_opposition_explanation: Kumar, whose singing partnership with Laxmi produces the misconception, and the years of separation in which she cannot be traced. There is no family veto or villain; the obstacle is a misunderstanding compounded by time.
lover_boy_explanation: The film is organised around a marriage and its recovery, and Vijay's whole late arc is the search for the wife he drove out, which is devotion of a kind. It is held at the midpoint because the defining act of the role is jealous expulsion rather than courtship or sacrifice.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kapoor was fifty and playing a professor confronting his own younger self in flashback, and the film leans on the song 'Patjhad Saawan Basant Bahaar' to carry what the couple have lost; the pairing works better in the recognition scenes than in the flashback marriage.
actor_transformation: From a husband who expels his wife on a suspicion to a man who spends years unable to find her and then resigns his post rather than face what he sees.
female_transformation: Laxmi leaves, raises their daughter alone in a widow's attire so that the child may be respectable, and finally explains the life she built to the husband who caused it.
relationship_outcome: Laxmi meets Vijay at his residence and tells him the truth about her widowhood; the film moves toward reunion.
relationship_analysis: The last romantic lead of Kapoor's Hindi career and his last commercial success, and a summary of the pattern the filmography keeps returning to: a marriage destroyed by a husband's misreading rather than by any external veto. The title, sindoor, names the vermilion of a married woman, which is precisely what Laxmi gives up in order to survive as a supposed widow.
critical_reading: The film treats Vijay's jealousy as a tragic error to be forgiven rather than as conduct with a cost, and the cost is borne entirely by Laxmi, who loses her home, her name and her profession and raises a daughter under a false widowhood. That she must adopt the appearance of a dead husband to be respectable is the sharpest thing in the film, and it is not presented as a criticism.

initial_relationship: Married for years and childless
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; the marriage is established when the film opens.
courtship_pattern: None. The film begins in a long marriage and ends it within its opening movement.
emotional_dynamic: Settled and close, and defined by a childlessness that finally resolves at the cost of her life.
pair_conflict: None between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict is recorded. The marriage is presented as close and untroubled, and what ends it is the childbirth she does not survive.
external_opposition_explanation: Years of childlessness, and then a pregnancy she is unlikely to survive. The opposition is entirely biological and it is fatal.
lover_boy_explanation: A husband rather than a suitor, with no courtship shown, but the role is organised around a promise made to a dying wife and kept for the rest of his life, which is constancy of a demonstrable kind. Scored below the midpoint because the devotion is expressed as celibacy and fatherhood rather than as romance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing, and the cast list marks Asha Parekh's appearance a guest role, so the couple have very little screen time together. The score reflects the slightness of the documented material rather than a judgement about the playing.
actor_transformation: From a husband of long standing to a widower raising a daughter alone under a promise never to marry again.
female_transformation: Suman bears the child she waited years for and, dying, extracts the promise that governs the rest of Kumar's life.
relationship_outcome: Ended by her death after childbirth; Kumar keeps the promise and never remarries.
relationship_analysis: The fourth and last Kapoor and Asha Parekh pairing, and by some distance the briefest: a guest appearance that dies in the opening movement and then governs the whole film through a deathbed promise. It belongs with Silsila and Aandhi-Toofan in the late group where his character's marriage exists chiefly to be lost.
critical_reading: A wife who waits years for a child, dies producing one, and binds her husband to lifelong celibacy is a construction the period used often, and the film treats the promise as touching rather than as a demand. Suman's one action in the film is to determine what her husband may do for the rest of his life, which is agency of a distinctly circumscribed kind.

initial_relationship: Married, living in a house near the railway station he runs
how_they_meet: Not dramatised; Motilal marries Sumita and they settle close to the station.
courtship_pattern: None shown. The marriage is established and the film observes what the station does to it.
emotional_dynamic: A settled marriage steadily undermined by the presence of another woman living on her husband's premises at his sufferance.
pair_conflict: Sumita suspects Motilal of an affair with Tulsi, the abandoned woman he has housed in the station waiting room, and the suspicion hardens when Tulsi becomes pregnant.
pair_friction_explanation: Sustained and corrosive: the article describes an ongoing distrust between the two women driven by Sumita's suspicion of her husband, running across years of the film's chronology. It stops short of the highest band because no rupture is recorded and because the article never confirms that the suspicion is well founded.
external_opposition_explanation: Tulsi's presence in the waiting room, which Motilal permits and which his marriage cannot absorb; Gupta, his supervisor, whose complaints force him to evict her; and the station itself, a workplace that is also his household's boundary.
lover_boy_explanation: A station master in a rural ensemble drama, with no courtship, declaration or romantic action of any kind. The part's moral interest is in what he owes a destitute woman, not in what he feels for his wife, and the romance register is absent.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Smita Patil died in 1986 while the film was still in production and it was not released until 1989, with the storyline altered around her death and Sanjeev Kumar's, so what survives of the marriage on screen is necessarily partial.
actor_transformation: From the station's quiet benefactor to the man who puts Tulsi out at his supervisor's insistence, with his marriage's suspicion unresolved.
female_transformation: Sumita moves from wife to the household's investigator, confronting Tulsi directly over the paternity of her child.
relationship_outcome: Not stated; the article's plot summary breaks off after years of accumulated tensions.
relationship_analysis: The last marriage of substance in the filmography, and one of the few in which Kapoor's character is suspected rather than wronged. It closes a line that runs from Aamne Samne through Satyam Shivam Sundaram and Sindoor: a marriage in which one partner cannot establish what the other has done, with the difference that here the doubt is the wife's and the film never resolves it in his favour.
critical_reading: The film sets two women against each other over a man who has authority over both the house and the waiting room, and it is Tulsi, with no standing at all, who is evicted when the institution objects. Sumita's suspicion is treated as the marriage's problem rather than as a reasonable response to her husband housing another woman indefinitely, and the plot's sympathy sits with Motilal's decency.
